questions.title: ROW_NUMBER vs. RANK vs. DENSE_RANK
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() in SQL Server. If two products are tied for the highest price, what number does each function give the row right after them?
questions.modelAnswer: All three are ranking window functions used with OVER(ORDER BY ...), and all three number rows based on the order you specify, but they disagree on what happens with ties. ROW_NUMBER() always assigns a unique, sequential integer to every row, even when two rows are tied on the ORDER BY column -- one of the tied rows arbitrarily gets the lower number. RANK() gives tied rows the same number, but then skips ahead by the size of the tie: if two rows tie for rank 1, the next distinct row gets rank 3, not 2, because RANK() is really counting 'how many rows came before or tied with me, plus one.' DENSE_RANK() also gives tied rows the same number, but the next distinct value gets the very next integer with no gap -- it's counting distinct values, not rows. So for two products tied for the most expensive: ROW_NUMBER gives them 1 and 2 (arbitrarily), RANK gives them both 1 and the next product gets 3, and DENSE_RANK gives them both 1 and the next product gets 2.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it with a concrete example because the difference only shows up when there's a tie. Say I'm ranking products by ListPrice and two products are tied for the top price. ROW_NUMBER() doesn't know about ties at all -- it just hands out 1, 2, 3, 4 in order, so the two tied products arbitrarily get 1 and 2. RANK() respects the tie -- both get rank 1 -- but it still 'reserves' a slot for each of them, so the next product down is rank 3, not 2. DENSE_RANK() is the one that feels most natural for something like a pricing tier: both tied products get 1, and the next distinct price is simply 2, no gap. In practice I reach for ROW_NUMBER() constantly for deduplication -- partition by the natural key, order by something like an ID, and anything with RowNum greater than 1 is a duplicate I can delete. I reach for RANK() when ties should genuinely cost a position, like a sales leaderboard where two reps tied for 2nd really does mean nobody is 3rd. And I reach for DENSE_RANK() when I just want the next distinct tier number and don't want gaps confusing anyone reading the report.
questions.example:
SELECT Name, ListPrice,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RowNum,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS Rank_,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS DenseRank_
FROM Production.Product
ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
-- If two products tie for the top ListPrice:
-- RowNum:     1, 2, 3, 4...  (ties broken arbitrarily)
-- Rank_:      1, 1, 3, 4...  (skips to 3 after the tie)
-- DenseRank_: 1, 1, 2, 3...  (no gap after the tie)
commonMistakes: Saying ROW_NUMBER() can produce duplicate numbers for ties (it never can -- it's always unique)
Mixing up which function skips numbers after a tie (it's RANK, not DENSE_RANK)
Forgetting that ROW_NUMBER() requires ORDER BY inside OVER() -- without it, row order is undefined
Not realizing all three still need PARTITION BY to restart numbering per group
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique numbers, ties broken arbitrarily
RANK() gives ties the same number and skips ahead by the tie size afterward
DENSE_RANK() gives ties the same number with no gap for the next distinct value
Choice depends on whether the business question treats a tie as 'costing' a rank

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes ROW_NUMBER's uniqueness behavior
Correctly describes RANK's gap-after-tie behavior
Correctly describes DENSE_RANK's no-gap behavior
Gives a realistic scenario for choosing one over another

questions.title: Transactions: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK
questions.prompt: Explain what a transaction is in SQL Server, what COMMIT does that running the statements without a transaction wouldn't, and what exactly ROLLBACK undoes.
questions.modelAnswer: A transaction groups one or more statements into a single all-or-nothing unit. BEGIN TRANSACTION marks the start of that group. Until COMMIT runs, the changes are provisional -- visible in the current session but not yet permanently saved, and still subject to being undone. COMMIT TRANSACTION makes every change inside the group permanent, all at once. ROLLBACK TRANSACTION undoes every change made since the matching BEGIN TRANSACTION, as if none of it had ever happened. The reason this matters: a multi-step change (like moving stock from one location to another with two separate UPDATE statements) can fail halfway through if run as two independent statements, leaving the data in an inconsistent state. Wrapping both statements in a transaction guarantees either both succeed or neither does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I usually explain this with the classic example: moving inventory from warehouse A to warehouse B is really two UPDATEs -- subtract from A, add to B. If I just run those as two separate statements and the second one fails, I've got stock that's vanished into nowhere. A transaction fixes that by treating both statements as one all-or-nothing unit. BEGIN TRANSACTION starts the clock; until I COMMIT, those changes are provisional -- I can see them in my own session, but they're not durably saved and SQL Server can still throw them away. COMMIT makes them permanent. ROLLBACK is the safety net -- if something goes wrong partway through, it undoes everything back to the BEGIN, cleanly, as if I'd never run anything at all. The discipline I bring to it professionally is keeping transactions as short as possible, because every lock held inside one is held until COMMIT or ROLLBACK runs.
commonMistakes: Thinking changes inside a transaction are already permanent before COMMIT runs
Forgetting that ROLLBACK undoes everything since BEGIN TRANSACTION, not just the most recent statement
Leaving a transaction open for a long time, holding locks and blocking other users unnecessarily
Not pairing every BEGIN TRANSACTION with a guaranteed COMMIT or ROLLBACK, even on the error path
keyPoints: A transaction is an all-or-nothing group of statements
Changes are provisional until COMMIT makes them permanent
ROLLBACK undoes everything since the matching BEGIN TRANSACTION
Transactions exist to prevent partial, inconsistent multi-step changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a transaction groups together
Correctly explains what COMMIT does and the provisional state before it
Correctly explains the scope of what ROLLBACK undoes
Gives a realistic scenario showing why this matters

questions.title: EXISTS vs. IN vs. JOIN for Existence Checks
questions.prompt: You need to find every customer who has placed at least one order. Compare writing this with EXISTS, with IN, and with an INNER JOIN plus DISTINCT. Explain how each one behaves when a customer has multiple orders, and the specific trap with NOT IN when the subquery's column can contain NULLs.
questions.modelAnswer: EXISTS, IN, and INNER JOIN with DISTINCT can all answer 'does this customer have at least one order,' but they get there differently. EXISTS(subquery) is a pure existence check -- SQL Server can stop scanning the moment it finds one matching row, and a customer with ten orders still only produces one result row, because EXISTS never actually returns the subquery's rows, just a true/false per outer row. IN (subquery) compares the outer column against the whole list the subquery returns; it also naturally avoids duplication since it's testing membership, not joining. An INNER JOIN behaves differently: joining Customer to Order on CustomerID and a customer with three orders produces three joined rows, which means DISTINCT (or GROUP BY) is required afterward to get back to one row per customer -- without it, the result silently overcounts. The sharper trap is with NOT IN rather than IN: if the subquery's column can contain a NULL, NOT IN against that list returns no rows at all for every single outer row, because SQL's three-valued logic can never prove an inequality against an unknown value. EXISTS doesn't have this problem because it's testing a condition, not comparing against a value list, which is one reason NOT EXISTS is generally the safer choice for 'does not have a match.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through why these three roads to the same destination aren't actually equivalent in practice. EXISTS is the one I reach for by default for a pure existence check -- it's a yes/no test, the optimizer can bail out the instant it finds one match, and a customer with ten orders still contributes exactly one row to the result, because EXISTS never pulls the subquery's actual data back. IN behaves similarly for this particular case -- it's checking membership in a list, not joining, so it also doesn't duplicate. Where people get burned is reaching for a plain INNER JOIN instead: the moment you join Customer to Order, a customer with three orders becomes three rows, and if you forget the DISTINCT, you've silently inflated your result set without an error anywhere to tell you. But the real gotcha I always bring up, because it's bitten people in production, is NOT IN with a nullable column -- if even one NULL sneaks into the subquery's result, NOT IN returns completely empty, for every row, with no warning. I treat that as a hard rule: never write NOT IN against a column that could contain NULL -- use NOT EXISTS instead, which doesn't have that failure mode at all.
questions.example:
-- EXISTS: pure existence check, no duplication risk
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM [Order] o WHERE o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID);

-- IN: membership test against the subquery's result list
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
WHERE c.CustomerID IN (SELECT o.CustomerID FROM [Order] o);

-- JOIN: requires DISTINCT or a customer with 3 orders appears 3 times
SELECT DISTINCT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
INNER JOIN [Order] o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID;

-- THE TRAP: if Order.CustomerID can be NULL, this returns ZERO rows for every customer:
SELECT c.CustomerID FROM Customer c
WHERE c.CustomerID NOT IN (SELECT o.CustomerID FROM [Order] o); -- avoid if nullable
commonMistakes: Writing a plain INNER JOIN for an existence check and forgetting DISTINCT, silently duplicating customers with multiple orders
Using NOT IN against a subquery column that can contain NULL, not realizing it returns zero rows for every outer row
Assuming EXISTS and IN always perform identically to a JOIN, when EXISTS can short-circuit and avoid materializing the whole list
Not recognizing that EXISTS never actually returns the subquery's column values -- only whether a match exists
keyPoints: EXISTS is a short-circuiting existence check; it returns one result row regardless of how many matches exist
IN compares against a list but doesn't duplicate rows the way a JOIN does
An INNER JOIN needs DISTINCT/GROUP BY to avoid duplicating a row per matching child record
NOT IN against a nullable column can return zero rows entirely -- NOT EXISTS avoids that trap

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains EXISTS's existence-check, non-duplicating behavior
Correctly explains why a JOIN needs DISTINCT to avoid duplication
Correctly identifies the NOT IN / NULL trap and why NOT EXISTS avoids it
Provides correct, illustrative SQL for at least two of the three approaches

questions.title: CTEs vs. Views: Same Shape, Different Lifetime
questions.prompt: A coworker says, "I don't get why we need views — a CTE already lets me name a subquery." Explain the real difference between a CTE and a view, and when you'd reach for one over the other.
questions.modelAnswer: A CTE and a view can look nearly identical — both let you name a SELECT and reference it like a table — but they differ in lifetime and scope. A CTE, defined with WITH, exists only for the single statement immediately following it; the moment that statement finishes, the CTE is gone, and no other query, session, or user can reference it. A view, created with CREATE VIEW, is a permanent database object: it's saved once and can be queried by name from any session, any user with permission, indefinitely, until someone runs DROP VIEW. Neither one stores actual data — both re-run their underlying SELECT against live data every time they're referenced. The practical rule: reach for a CTE to make one complex query more readable, especially when you need to reference the same intermediate result twice in that query. Reach for a view when the same logic needs to be reused across many different queries, by many different people or tools, including reporting tools like Power BI connecting directly to the database.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with the one-sentence version first: a CTE lives for one statement, a view lives forever until someone deletes it. If I'm writing a gnarly query with three levels of nested subqueries and I just want to name the middle layer so I can read my own logic back, that's a CTE — it's disposable, scoped to right here, right now. But if I've built a 'active customers with more than $1,000 in lifetime orders' query that three different reports are going to need, I don't want three copies of that logic drifting out of sync — I'd save it once as a view, under a clear name, so every query and every person on the team references the same definition. I'd also mention that a view is a real object other tools can see too — if a BI tool is connecting directly to the database instead of importing through a query editor, it can query a view exactly like a table, which a CTE could never support.
questions.example:
-- CTE: scoped to this one statement only
WITH RecentOrders AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, SUM(TotalDue) AS Total
    FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
    WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01'
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)
SELECT * FROM RecentOrders WHERE Total > 5000;
-- RecentOrders no longer exists after this statement runs.

-- View: saved permanently, reusable by anyone with access
CREATE VIEW vw_RecentOrderTotals AS
SELECT CustomerID, SUM(TotalDue) AS Total
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01'
GROUP BY CustomerID;

SELECT * FROM vw_RecentOrderTotals WHERE Total > 5000;
commonMistakes: Assuming a CTE can be reused across multiple separate statements or sessions (it can't)
Assuming either one stores a physical copy of the data (both re-run their SELECT live)
Reaching for a view for a one-off readability fix inside a single complex query, when a CTE is simpler and doesn't leave a permanent object behind
Forgetting that a view is directly queryable by reporting tools connecting to the database, the way a CTE never could be
keyPoints: A CTE is scoped to one statement; a view persists until explicitly dropped
Neither stores data — both run their SELECT fresh against live data each time
CTEs suit one-off readability inside a single complex query
Views suit logic that needs to be reused across many queries, people, or tools

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains a CTE's one-statement lifetime
Correctly explains a view's persistent, reusable lifetime
States that neither stores data, both re-run live
Gives a realistic scenario for choosing one over the other

questions.title: What Makes a Window Function Different from GROUP BY
questions.prompt: Explain how a window function using OVER() differs from GROUP BY, and why you might reach for AVG(Price) OVER (PARTITION BY Category) instead of a GROUP BY query, even though both compute an average per category.
questions.modelAnswer: GROUP BY and a window function can compute the exact same aggregate — an average per category — but they do fundamentally different things to the result set. GROUP BY collapses every row in a group down into a single summary row, so a table of 500 products grouped by category becomes a handful of rows, one per category, with the individual products gone. A window function, triggered by adding OVER() to an aggregate, computes the same aggregate across a group of related rows but keeps every original row intact in the output — nothing collapses. PARTITION BY inside OVER() divides rows into groups purely for that calculation's purpose, exactly like GROUP BY divides rows, but the row-level result is untouched. The practical reason to reach for the window function version: you need the category average sitting alongside each individual product's own price, for example to compute how far above or below that category's average a specific product is priced — a comparison GROUP BY's collapsed output couldn't support at all, since the individual product's own price no longer exists in a grouped result.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start with what actually happens to the rows, because that's the real distinction, not just syntax. GROUP BY by category gives me one row per category — Bikes, Accessories, Clothing — and the individual products are gone from the output. AVG(Price) OVER (PARTITION BY Category) gives me back every single product row, but now each one also carries its own category's average price as an extra column sitting right next to it. That's the whole reason I'd reach for the window function version: I usually want to compare something at the row level against a group-level number — 'how does this specific product's price compare to the average for its category?' — and I can only do that math if both numbers are available on the same row. If all I actually need is the category averages themselves, with no individual rows attached, plain GROUP BY is simpler and I wouldn't bother with OVER() at all.
questions.example:
-- GROUP BY: collapses to one row per category
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, AVG(ListPrice) AS AvgPrice
FROM Production.Product
GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID;

-- Window function: keeps every product row, adds the category average alongside it
SELECT Name, ProductSubcategoryID, ListPrice,
       AVG(ListPrice) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductSubcategoryID) AS AvgPriceForCategory,
       ListPrice - AVG(ListPrice) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductSubcategoryID) AS DiffFromAvg
FROM Production.Product;
commonMistakes: Saying GROUP BY and a window function always return the same number of rows (GROUP BY collapses; a window function does not)
Forgetting PARTITION BY is required to restart the calculation per group, not just ORDER BY
Assuming a window function requires an aggregate you can't also compute with GROUP BY — the aggregate itself is identical, only the row-collapsing behavior differs
Using GROUP BY when the goal was actually a row-level comparison against a group total, then wondering why the individual values disappeared
keyPoints: GROUP BY collapses rows into one summary row per group
A window function (OVER()) keeps every original row while still computing a per-group aggregate
PARTITION BY divides rows into groups for the window calculation only, without collapsing anything
Choose the window function when you need a row-level value compared against a group-level aggregate

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains GROUP BY's row-collapsing behavior
Correctly explains that a window function preserves every row
Correctly describes PARTITION BY's role
Gives a realistic scenario where the window function's row-level detail matters

questions.title: withColumn() vs. select() for Adding a Derived Column
questions.prompt: In PySpark, you need to add a new column to a DataFrame that's a tax-adjusted version of an existing Price column. Explain the difference between doing this with withColumn() and doing it with select(), and why calling withColumn() in a tight loop to add dozens of columns one at a time is a performance anti-pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: withColumn() adds or replaces exactly one named column while implicitly keeping every other column as-is -- it's the natural choice when you just need to bolt one derived value onto an otherwise unchanged DataFrame. select() instead requires you to explicitly list every column you want in the output, including the ones you're keeping unchanged, alongside the new expression -- more to type, but it makes the full resulting shape explicit in one line. The performance issue isn't withColumn() itself, it's calling it repeatedly in a loop: each call adds another Project node to Spark's logical plan, and chaining dozens of them one at a time builds a deeply nested plan that the Catalyst optimizer has to analyze, which can become genuinely slow (and in extreme cases has caused analysis errors) as the chain grows. The fix is building all the new column expressions up front and applying them together in a single select(), rather than looping withColumn() calls one column at a time.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain withColumn() as the 'just this one column' tool -- call it once, give it a name and an expression, and everything else on the DataFrame passes through untouched. select() is the 'describe the whole output' tool -- I have to name every column I want, including ones I'm not changing, but in exchange I get a single line that says exactly what the result looks like. Where this actually matters in practice is when someone writes a for loop that calls withColumn() once per new column needed -- maybe 30 times -- because each one of those calls adds another layer to the query plan, and that nested plan gets genuinely expensive to analyze as it grows. I'd batch all 30 derived expressions into a list and apply them in one select() call instead, which produces the identical result with one pass through plan analysis instead of 30.
questions.example:
# Fine for a single derived column:
df2 = df.withColumn("PriceWithTax", col("Price") * 1.08)

# Equivalent, explicit full-shape version with select():
df2 = df.select("*", (col("Price") * 1.08).alias("PriceWithTax"))

# ANTI-PATTERN: looping withColumn() to add many columns one at a time
for new_col, expr in many_derived_columns.items():
    df = df.withColumn(new_col, expr)   # builds a deeply nested plan

# BETTER: batch all expressions into one select()
df = df.select("*", *[expr.alias(name) for name, expr in many_derived_columns.items()])
commonMistakes: Believing withColumn() always recomputes the whole DataFrame expensively, when the real cost is calling it repeatedly in a loop, not using it once
Not realizing select() requires explicitly naming every column you want to keep
Building 30+ sequential withColumn() calls in a loop instead of batching into one select()
Assuming the two approaches produce different results when used correctly for a single column add
keyPoints: withColumn() adds or replaces one named column while implicitly keeping all others
select() requires explicitly listing every column kept, but makes the full output shape explicit
Calling withColumn() repeatedly in a loop builds a deeply nested plan that slows analysis
The fix is batching many column expressions into a single select() call

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains withColumn()'s single-column add/replace behavior
Correctly explains select()'s explicit-column-list requirement
Correctly explains why looping withColumn() calls is a performance anti-pattern
Provides correct, relevant PySpark example code

questions.title: What MERGE INTO Actually Does in Delta Lake
questions.prompt: Explain what MERGE INTO does in Delta Lake, specifically how it decides whether to update an existing row or insert a new one, and why MERGE is preferred over a separate DELETE-then-INSERT for upserting changed records into a Delta table.
questions.modelAnswer: MERGE INTO performs an atomic upsert: it joins a source dataset to a target Delta table on a specified matching condition, and for rows where a match is found, applies the WHEN MATCHED clause (typically an UPDATE SET); for rows in the source with no match in the target, it applies WHEN NOT MATCHED (typically an INSERT); an optional WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE clause can handle target rows missing from the new source, for a full three-way sync including deletes. The whole operation runs inside a single Delta transaction captured in the transaction log, meaning other readers never see a partial state -- some rows updated, some not yet inserted. A separate DELETE followed by an INSERT is two independent transactions: a reader querying between them could see data missing entirely, and a failure between the two leaves the table in a genuinely inconsistent state. MERGE also typically performs better, because Delta's engine can target only the files actually touched by matching rows, rather than rewriting broader chunks of the table across two separate operations.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe MERGE INTO as one atomic statement doing the work that DELETE-then-INSERT tries to do with two. It joins my incoming source data to the existing target table on whatever key identifies a row -- customer_id, order_id, whatever -- and for every row where that join finds a match, it runs the UPDATE I specified; for every source row with no match, it runs the INSERT instead. Because this all happens as one transaction recorded in Delta's log, nobody querying the table mid-operation ever sees a half-finished state, which DELETE-then-INSERT genuinely can't promise -- there's a real window between the DELETE committing and the INSERT committing where the data looks wrong or missing to anyone reading at that exact moment. I'd also mention the full-sync variant, WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE, which lets MERGE handle deletions too when the source represents the complete current state rather than just a batch of changes.
questions.example:
MERGE INTO customers AS t
USING updates AS s
ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;
commonMistakes: Thinking MERGE requires two separate passes over the data the way DELETE+INSERT does
Forgetting the ON condition must uniquely identify a row, or multiple source rows matching one target row causes an error
Using DELETE+INSERT and exposing a partial state to concurrent readers between the two statements
Forgetting WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE exists for the delete side of a full three-way sync
keyPoints: MERGE INTO is a single atomic transaction joining source to target
WHEN MATCHED updates existing rows; WHEN NOT MATCHED inserts new ones
Atomicity is the real advantage over DELETE+INSERT, not just convenience
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE supports deletes in a full sync pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the join plus WHEN MATCHED/NOT MATCHED mechanics
Correctly explains the atomicity advantage over DELETE+INSERT
Mentions WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE or an equivalent nuance
Provides correct, valid example syntax

questions.title: Querying a Delta Table's Past State With Time Travel
questions.prompt: Explain how Delta Lake's time travel feature works under the hood -- what makes it possible for VERSION AS OF 5 or TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-01-01' to return the table exactly as it looked at that point -- and what actually limits how far back you can time travel.
questions.modelAnswer: Delta Lake maintains a transaction log (the _delta_log directory) recording every committed operation against the table, where each commit records exactly which data files were added and which were logically removed, rather than mutating files in place. Time travel works by replaying the transaction log up to a specific version number or timestamp and reconstructing the set of data files that were 'live' at that point, then reading only those files -- it's not a special stored snapshot, it's a deterministic replay of history that already exists. What actually limits how far back you can go is the VACUUM command: VACUUM physically deletes data files no longer referenced by the current table version that are older than the retention threshold (default 7 days), so after a VACUUM, versions that depended on those now-deleted files can no longer be reconstructed, producing an error rather than wrong data.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain that Delta doesn't keep a separate full copy of the table for every version -- that would be enormously wasteful. Instead, every write operation is recorded as a commit in the transaction log that says exactly which Parquet files became part of the table and which ones stopped being part of it. VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF just replays that log up to the point requested and figures out which files were live at that moment, then reads only those. The thing that actually caps how far back this works is VACUUM -- it physically deletes files that are old and no longer referenced by the current version, and once it's run, any older version that needed those files for its reconstruction simply can't be read anymore. That's why I always treat the default 7-day retention as the real boundary on how useful time travel is for anything beyond short-term auditing or undoing a recent mistake.
commonMistakes: Thinking Delta stores a separate full copy of the table for every version
Forgetting VACUUM can permanently remove the files a time-travel query would need
Assuming time travel works indefinitely into the past regardless of retention settings
Confusing VERSION AS OF (a commit number) with TIMESTAMP AS OF (wall-clock time), which can resolve to a nearby commit rather than an exact one
keyPoints: Time travel replays the transaction log's record of added/removed files, it's not a stored snapshot copy
Each commit lists exactly which files became live and which were logically removed
VACUUM is what actually limits history by physically deleting old, unreferenced files
Default retention is 7 days, after which older versions may become unreadable

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the transaction log's add/remove file record as the mechanism
Correctly explains VACUUM as the real limiting factor
Provides correct VERSION AS OF / TIMESTAMP AS OF syntax
Notes the default retention period or a similar relevant detail

questions.title: What OPTIMIZE and ZORDER BY Actually Fix
questions.prompt: A Delta table that's loaded via thousands of small streaming micro-batch writes has gotten noticeably slower to query. Explain what problem OPTIMIZE solves here, and what ZORDER BY adds on top of plain OPTIMIZE.
questions.modelAnswer: Many small writes -- one tiny file per micro-batch -- create the classic 'small file problem': querying the table means opening and reading metadata for thousands of tiny files instead of a smaller number of appropriately-sized ones, and that per-file overhead dominates query time long before the actual data volume justifies it. OPTIMIZE performs file compaction (bin-packing): it rewrites many small files into a smaller number of larger, right-sized files (around 1GB by default), without changing the table's data or history, directly reducing that per-file overhead. ZORDER BY adds a second improvement on top: it co-locates rows with similar values in the specified column(s) within the same files during that same rewrite, so a query filtering on that column can skip entire files that provably don't contain matching values (data skipping), rather than just benefiting from fewer, bigger files. ZORDER is most valuable on columns frequently used in WHERE clauses with high cardinality; it's wasted on a column that's already naturally clustered or rarely filtered on.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd name this as the small-file problem right away, because that's exactly what thousands of tiny streaming-batch files produce -- every query has to open and read metadata for far more files than the actual data volume warrants, and that overhead is what's actually slowing things down, not the data itself. OPTIMIZE fixes that specific problem by rewriting those small files into a smaller number of properly-sized ones, with no change to the table's logical data or its history. ZORDER BY is a second, separate improvement I'd add on top when queries also filter heavily on a specific column -- it arranges the rewrite so rows with similar values in that column end up physically co-located in the same files, which lets Delta's data-skipping feature avoid opening files that can't possibly contain what the query's looking for. I'd be specific that ZORDER only earns its cost on a column that's actually filtered on often and has enough distinct values to make the co-location meaningful -- running it on a low-cardinality or rarely-filtered column is just wasted rewrite work.
questions.example:
OPTIMIZE events;
OPTIMIZE events ZORDER BY (user_id);
commonMistakes: Thinking ZORDER BY is required to get any benefit from OPTIMIZE, when plain OPTIMIZE alone fixes the small-file problem
ZORDER-ing a column that's rarely filtered on, wasting the rewrite with no real query benefit
Assuming OPTIMIZE changes query results or deletes history (it doesn't -- old files just become unreferenced, cleaned up later by VACUUM)
Not running OPTIMIZE regularly on a frequently-streamed-into table, letting the small-file problem recur
keyPoints: Many small files from streaming writes create per-file overhead that slows queries (the small file problem)
OPTIMIZE bin-packs small files into fewer, right-sized files
ZORDER BY co-locates similar values so filtering queries can skip irrelevant files (data skipping)
ZORDER is most valuable on frequently-filtered, high-cardinality columns

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the small-file problem
Correctly explains what OPTIMIZE's compaction does
Correctly explains what ZORDER BY adds (data skipping via co-location)
Notes when ZORDER is or isn't worth applying

questions.title: What Each Medallion Layer Is Actually Responsible For
questions.prompt: A junior engineer asks why a pipeline needs three separate layers (bronze, silver, gold) instead of just cleaning and aggregating the data in one pass straight from the source. Explain what each layer is actually responsible for, and the real reason for keeping them separate.
questions.modelAnswer: Bronze holds raw data close to its original source format, ingested with minimal or no transformation -- the goal is a faithful, replayable copy of exactly what arrived, including bad rows and duplicates, because that's what lets you reprocess from scratch if downstream logic turns out to be wrong. Silver applies cleaning, conforming, deduplication, and standard business keys/types -- it's queryable, trustworthy data, but still close to record-level grain, not yet aggregated for a specific business question. Gold applies business-level aggregation and modeling -- star schemas, pre-aggregated metrics -- shaped specifically for how a particular dashboard or report will consume it. The real reason to keep them separate rather than one combined pass: if a transformation bug is discovered in the gold aggregation logic three weeks later, having bronze still intact means reprocessing from the original raw data is possible; if the first pass already overwrote or discarded the raw form, that bug could mean a permanently lost ability to correctly reconstruct history.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them the three layers aren't about following a convention, they're about not losing the ability to fix a mistake. Bronze is the one copy I keep as close to the original source as possible -- messy, duplicated, whatever it actually looked like coming in -- specifically so that if something downstream turns out wrong, I can reprocess from a faithful starting point instead of from already-transformed data that might be missing exactly what I'd need. Silver is where I actually clean things up -- dedup, standardize types, conform keys -- but I keep it at roughly record-level grain rather than jumping straight to a specific report's shape, because other things besides that one report might need this same clean, record-level data. Gold is the layer that's actually shaped for a specific consumer -- a dashboard, an aggregate table a report queries directly. If I collapsed all three into one pass straight from source, and I find a bug in my aggregation logic three weeks from now, I've got nothing faithful left to reprocess from -- that's the real cost of skipping the separation, not just tidiness.

Skipping silver and aggregating straight to gold, losing a trustworthy, record-level layer for ad hoc questions
Assuming the three layers are just a naming convention rather than reflecting a real reprocessing/lineage benefit
Applying business-specific aggregation logic in silver, coupling a shared layer to one dashboard's needs

Silver is cleaned, deduplicated, record-level data, not yet aggregated for one specific use
Gold is business-level, aggregated, and shaped for specific consumption
Separation protects against unrecoverable mistakes discovered downstream

questions.title: Glue Crawler vs. Glue ETL Job: What Each One Actually Does
questions.prompt: A coworker says, "We don't need an ETL job -- the crawler already read the data." Explain what a Glue Crawler actually does versus what a Glue ETL job does, and why running a crawler alone is never sufficient to transform data.
questions.modelAnswer: A Crawler's job is purely about metadata: it connects to a data store (S3, a JDBC source, etc.), infers schema -- column names and types -- detects partition structure, and writes or updates table definitions in the Glue Data Catalog. It never reads the data in order to change it, only to describe it. A Glue ETL job is a different thing entirely: a Spark (or Python shell) job that actually reads the source data, applies transformations -- type casting, joins, deduplication, aggregation -- and writes a new output dataset somewhere. Running a crawler alone leaves you with Catalog entries pointing at the data exactly as it already was; Athena or Redshift Spectrum can now query that raw data because the Catalog knows its shape, but nothing about the underlying data itself has been cleaned, joined, or reshaped. The confusion usually comes from both sitting under the same "Glue" umbrella in the console -- a crawler discovers and describes, a job transforms and writes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct this gently but directly, because it's a really common mix-up early on. A crawler is a metadata operation -- it looks at files sitting in S3, figures out their schema and partition layout, and registers that as a table in the Data Catalog. It never touches the actual bytes of the data to change them. An ETL job is the thing that actually does the work people usually mean by "transform" -- reading the source, running real logic like dedup or joins or type fixes, and writing a new result. So if someone just ran a crawler and thinks the data's been processed, what's actually happened is: Athena can now query the raw file as a table, because the Catalog knows its columns, but the file itself is bit-for-bit identical to what landed in S3. If the raw data is messy -- inconsistent types, duplicates, nulls that need handling -- a crawler running on top of it will faithfully catalog that same mess; it has no concept of "clean this up," only "describe what's here."
commonMistakes: Assuming a crawler changes or cleans the underlying data, when it only catalogs it
Thinking Athena querying a crawled table means the data has been validated or transformed
Running a crawler repeatedly expecting it to eventually produce clean data on its own
Confusing the Data Catalog (a metadata store) with an actual processed dataset
keyPoints: A crawler infers and registers schema/partitions in the Glue Data Catalog -- a metadata-only operation
A Glue ETL job actually reads, transforms, and writes data
Crawling alone makes raw data queryable, not clean or transformed
Both sit under 'Glue' in the console, which is a common source of the confusion

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the Crawler's metadata-only role
Correctly explains what an ETL job actually does differently
Explains why crawling alone doesn't transform data
Notes the common source of the confusion

questions.title: Redshift Distribution Styles at a Glance: KEY, ALL, and EVEN
questions.prompt: Explain the three Redshift distribution styles -- KEY, ALL, and EVEN -- at a glance: what each one does to how rows land across compute nodes, and which one you'd pick for a small, frequently-joined dimension table versus a large fact table joined on customer_id.
questions.modelAnswer: DISTSTYLE EVEN spreads rows round-robin across all slices with no awareness of how the table will be joined -- simple, but it gives no join-locality benefit. DISTSTYLE KEY hashes rows on a specified distribution key column, so every row with the same key value lands on the same slice; the point is making a join on that key a local, same-slice operation instead of requiring data to be shuffled across the network at query time. DISTSTYLE ALL copies the entire table to every node -- wasteful for a large table, but ideal for a small table that gets joined constantly, since every slice already holds a full local copy and never needs to fetch matching rows from elsewhere. For a small, frequently-joined dimension table: ALL, since the storage cost of a few full copies is trivial and every join against it becomes local. For a large fact table joined on customer_id: KEY distribution on customer_id, so that matching rows on both sides of that join co-locate on the same slice and the join avoids a network shuffle.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through these by what actually happens to a row physically, since that's the part people skip. EVEN is the simplest -- round-robin, no thought given to how the table gets queried, which is fine for a table that's rarely joined but a missed opportunity for one that is. KEY is the one that actually optimizes for joins: pick the column the table is most often joined on, hash rows on it, and now a join against another table distributed the same way on the same key doesn't need to move data across the network at query time -- it's already sitting on the same slice. ALL is for small reference tables -- a dimension table with a few thousand rows costs almost nothing to fully replicate onto every node, and in exchange every join against it, from any fact table, is local no matter how that fact table itself is distributed. For the specific scenario here, I'd put the dimension table on ALL and the fact table on KEY(customer_id) -- assuming customer_id is genuinely the fact table's dominant join column -- rather than defaulting both to EVEN out of indecision.
commonMistakes: Defaulting every table to EVEN distribution without considering actual join patterns
Using ALL on a large, frequently-growing table, which multiplies storage and slows every write
Picking a KEY distribution column that isn't actually the dominant join column, gaining no real benefit
Assuming distribution style only affects storage, not query performance via join locality
keyPoints: EVEN spreads rows round-robin with no join awareness
KEY hashes on a chosen column so matching join keys co-locate on the same slice
ALL replicates the full table to every node, ideal for small, frequently-joined tables
Choice should be driven by actual join patterns and table size, not a default habit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains EVEN distribution's behavior
Correctly explains KEY distribution and its join-locality purpose
Correctly explains ALL distribution and when it's appropriate
Correctly applies the choice to the dimension-vs-fact scenario given

questions.title: Why Athena Charges Per Terabyte Scanned, and What Partitioning Actually Fixes
questions.prompt: Athena bills per terabyte of data scanned, not per query run. Explain why a poorly partitioned table makes that bill worse, and how partitioning, plus a columnar format like Parquet, actually fixes it.
questions.modelAnswer: Athena has no persistent indexes of its own -- every query reads through the underlying S3 files that could possibly be relevant, and the bill is calculated directly from how many bytes it had to read to answer the query. Without partitioning, a query filtering for one day's data still has to scan every file in the table, because there's no metadata telling Athena which files it can skip -- it must open and read all of them to find the matching rows. Partitioning the table by a column like order_date (reflected as folder structure in S3, e.g. order_date=2026-01-15/) lets Athena use partition metadata to skip entire folders of files that can't possibly match the query's filter, scanning only the relevant date's files instead of the whole table -- this is the single biggest cost lever for a table that's queried with date or category filters. Switching from a row-based format like CSV or JSON to a columnar format like Parquet adds a second, independent saving: a query that only needs three of forty columns can skip reading the bytes for the other thirty-seven entirely, something a row-based format can't do since every row's full set of columns is stored together.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the mental model first: Athena doesn't have indexes, so 'scanned' really does mean every byte it had to physically read off S3 to answer the query, and that's exactly what the bill is based on. If a table isn't partitioned, filtering for yesterday's orders still means Athena opens every file the table has, because nothing tells it which files are safe to skip -- there's no shortcut, it just has to check. Partitioning fixes that specific problem: once the S3 folder structure itself encodes the date, Athena can look at the query's filter, see it only needs the order_date=2026-01-15 folder, and skip every other folder's files without opening them at all. That alone is usually the biggest win. The second lever, separate from partitioning, is file format -- Parquet stores data column by column, so a query selecting three columns out of forty only has to read those three columns' bytes, not the whole row. CSV or JSON can't do that; every row's full width gets read regardless of which columns you actually asked for. I'd treat both as standard practice on any table that gets queried repeatedly, not just a performance nice-to-have.
commonMistakes: Assuming Athena has indexes the way a traditional database does, rather than scanning files directly
Leaving a large, frequently-filtered table unpartitioned and being surprised by the bill
Thinking partitioning alone is sufficient and ignoring the separate columnar-format saving
Partitioning on a column that's rarely filtered on, gaining none of the skip-folder benefit
keyPoints: Athena's cost is based directly on bytes scanned from S3, with no indexes to shortcut that
Partitioning lets Athena skip entire folders of files that can't match the query's filter
A columnar format like Parquet lets a query skip unneeded columns' bytes entirely
Partitioning and columnar format are two independent, stacking cost/performance levers

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why Athena's cost is tied to bytes scanned
Correctly explains how partitioning reduces scanned data via folder skipping
Correctly explains the separate columnar-format saving
Notes the two optimizations are independent and stack

questions.title: Top-2-per-group with a window function
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012's Production.Product table that returns the two highest-priced products in each color, without using a correlated subquery.
questions.modelAnswer: The idiomatic way to solve 'top N per group' in T-SQL is PARTITION BY plus ROW_NUMBER(), wrapped in a CTE so the ranking column can be filtered afterward. PARTITION BY Color restarts the numbering at 1 for each color, and ORDER BY ListPrice DESC makes 1 the most expensive product in that color. You can't filter directly on ROW_NUMBER() in the same SELECT's WHERE clause because window functions are logically evaluated after WHERE -- that's why the CTE (or a subquery) is necessary.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic 'top N per group' problem, and the pattern I reach for every time is a CTE with ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by the grouping column. I avoid a correlated subquery with TOP 2 inside it because that approach re-executes once per outer row and doesn't scale well. Instead, I compute the rank once in a CTE, then just filter WHERE RankInColor <= 2 in the outer query. The one gotcha I always mention out loud in an interview: you cannot write WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) <= 2 directly in the same SELECT, because the WHERE clause is logically evaluated before window functions are computed -- that's exactly why the CTE wrapper is required, not just a style preference.
questions.example:
WITH Ranked AS (
    SELECT Name, Color, ListPrice,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Color ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RankInColor
    FROM Production.Product
)
SELECT Name, Color, ListPrice
FROM Ranked
WHERE RankInColor <= 2
ORDER BY Color, RankInColor;
-- The CTE is required because ROW_NUMBER() can't be filtered in the same SELECT's WHERE clause.
commonMistakes: Trying to filter WHERE ROW_NUMBER() <= 2 directly in the same SELECT (not legal -- window functions evaluate after WHERE)
Forgetting PARTITION BY and ranking across the whole table instead of per color
Using TOP 2 with a correlated subquery per group, which is correct but far less efficient on large tables
Omitting ORDER BY inside OVER(), which leaves 'top' undefined
keyPoints: PARTITION BY restarts the ranking per group (per color here)
A CTE or subquery is required to filter on the window function's result
ORDER BY DESC inside OVER() makes rank 1 the highest price
This pattern generalizes to any 'top N per group' business question

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses ROW_NUMBER() with correct PARTITION BY and ORDER BY
Wraps it in a CTE/subquery to filter correctly
Query is syntactically valid and returns exactly 2 rows per color
Explains why filtering can't happen in the same SELECT's WHERE clause

questions.title: Temp table, table variable, or CTE?
questions.prompt: You need to hold an intermediate result set of about 500,000 rows, reuse it across three separate statements in a stored procedure, and would benefit from adding your own index to it. Which of #temp table, @table variable, or CTE would you choose, and why would the other two be worse choices here?
questions.modelAnswer: A #temp table is the right choice. It's a real, physically-stored table in tempdb, so SQL Server maintains real statistics on it (row counts), which lets the optimizer build a much smarter plan for a large result set, and you can explicitly add your own indexes to it. A table variable would be the wrong choice here: it also lives in tempdb, but historically has no maintained statistics, so on older compatibility levels the optimizer may assume just one row and badly under-allocate resources for 500,000 rows -- and while you can add inline PRIMARY KEY/UNIQUE constraints, you can't add arbitrary indexes the way you can on a #temp table. A CTE would also be the wrong choice: it isn't physically stored at all -- it's inlined into the query -- so referencing it in three separate statements could mean SQL Server re-runs its underlying query multiple times, and you can't add an index to something that was never materialized.
questions.professionalAnswer: Given the three constraints in the question -- large row count, reused across multiple statements, and wanting an index -- a #temp table wins on all three. The decision rule I use: CTEs are for one-time readability or recursion, not for reuse -- a CTE doesn't store anything, it's re-inlined at every reference, so touching it from three separate statements risks the underlying query running three separate times. Table variables are for small result sets inside a procedure where I want to avoid plan recompiles -- but historically they carry no real statistics, so the optimizer can badly misjudge a large one. A #temp table is the one option that's physically stored with real statistics the optimizer can use, and the only one of the three where I can explicitly add an index after the fact. For 500,000 rows reused three times, I'm reaching for #temp every time.
commonMistakes: Choosing a CTE for something reused across multiple statements, not realizing it may re-run its query each time
Choosing a table variable for a large result set, assuming it always performs the same as a temp table
Not mentioning that #temp tables maintain real statistics while table variables historically don't
Forgetting that CTEs can't be indexed at all, since nothing is actually materialized
keyPoints: #Temp tables are physically stored with maintained statistics and can be indexed
Table variables historically lack statistics, risking a poor plan on large sets
CTEs are inlined, not stored, and may re-execute their query on every reference
Choice depends on size, reuse, and whether an index is needed

Correctly explains why a table variable would be worse here
Correctly explains why a CTE would be worse here

questions.title: Raising a custom business-rule error
questions.prompt: Write T-SQL that checks whether a discount percentage exceeds 50% and, if so, raises a custom error using the modern recommended syntax. Then show how you would log an error inside a CATCH block and still let it propagate to the caller.
questions.modelAnswer: THROW is the modern, recommended way to raise a custom error, taking an error number, a message, and a state, and raising it exactly as if SQL Server had generated it itself. For a business rule like a discount cap, you check the condition and THROW a custom error if it's violated. To log an error and still propagate it, use THROW with no arguments inside a CATCH block -- it re-raises the exact error that was just caught, unmodified, after whatever logging or cleanup logic runs first. RAISERROR is the older syntax, still common in existing code, with a different argument shape (message, severity, state) -- recognize it, but prefer THROW for new code.
questions.professionalAnswer: For the business rule check itself, I'd write a simple IF that tests the discount, and THROW a custom error number with a clear message if it's violated -- that's the modern, recommended way, and it's a one-liner. The more interesting half of this question is re-throwing from a CATCH block, because that's a pattern people often get wrong: they either swallow the error silently after logging it, or they try to reconstruct it with a new THROW statement and lose the original error details. The clean way is TRY/CATCH around the risky operation, log whatever you need to inside CATCH, and then just write THROW with no arguments -- that re-raises the exact error that was caught, unmodified, so the caller still sees the real failure instead of a sanitized stand-in.
questions.example:
-- Business rule check
IF @DiscountPercent > 50
    THROW 50000, 'Discount cannot exceed 50 percent.', 1;

-- Logging then re-throwing the original error
BEGIN TRY
    UPDATE Sales.SpecialOffer SET DiscountPct = @DiscountPercent WHERE SpecialOfferID = @ID;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    INSERT INTO ErrorLog (ErrorMessage, LoggedAt) VALUES (ERROR_MESSAGE(), GETDATE());
    THROW; -- re-raises the exact caught error, unmodified
END CATCH
commonMistakes: Using RAISERROR for new code instead of the modern, recommended THROW
Writing a new THROW statement inside CATCH instead of bare THROW, which loses the original error's details
Forgetting THROW's argument order is (error number, message, state) -- a different shape than RAISERROR's
Swallowing the error entirely after logging it, instead of re-throwing so the caller knows it failed
keyPoints: THROW is the modern, recommended way to raise a custom error
Bare THROW inside CATCH re-raises the exact original error
RAISERROR is the older syntax, still seen in legacy code
Logging an error doesn't have to mean swallowing it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses THROW to raise a custom business-rule error
Correctly uses TRY/CATCH with bare THROW to re-raise after logging
Explains the difference between THROW and RAISERROR
Code is syntactically valid T-SQL

questions.title: Join Four Tables, Mixing INNER and LEFT
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012 that returns each order line's product name, order date, and the customer's first and last name, including order lines for products that may no longer have a subcategory assigned. Use at least one LEFT JOIN alongside INNER JOINs.
questions.modelAnswer: This requires chaining four tables together: SalesOrderHeader (for the order date and customer link), SalesOrderDetail (the order lines), Product (for the product name), and Person (for the customer's name), while also reaching ProductSubcategory with a LEFT JOIN so that products missing a subcategory still appear instead of being silently excluded. Each JOIN connects to whatever table already has the needed column available, not necessarily the very first table named in FROM — for instance, the join to Product uses ProductID from SalesOrderDetail, introduced by the join just before it. The LEFT JOIN to ProductSubcategory is the one deliberate choice: an INNER JOIN there would drop any order line whose product has a NULL ProductSubcategoryID, which is exactly the scenario the question asks to preserve.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this one join at a time rather than writing the whole thing at once, because that's the only way to keep four tables straight. I start from SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail joined on SalesOrderID, since that's the backbone of the query. Then I bring in Product on ProductID to get the product name, and Person on CustomerID (really BusinessEntityID) to get the name. All three of those are INNER JOINs because I genuinely need a match on all of them for the row to make sense. The one place I'd stop and think is ProductSubcategory — the question specifically says some products might not have one, and an INNER JOIN there would quietly drop those order lines from the result with no warning. That's exactly the signal to use LEFT JOIN instead, so a product with a NULL ProductSubcategoryID still shows up, just with NULL in the subcategory column rather than vanishing from the report entirely.
questions.example:
SELECT soh.OrderDate, p.Name AS ProductName, per.FirstName, per.LastName, ps.Name AS SubcategoryName
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader AS soh
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON soh.SalesOrderID = sod.SalesOrderID
INNER JOIN Production.Product AS p
    ON sod.ProductID = p.ProductID
INNER JOIN Person.Person AS per
    ON soh.CustomerID = per.BusinessEntityID
LEFT JOIN Production.ProductSubcategory AS ps
    ON p.ProductSubcategoryID = ps.ProductSubcategoryID;
commonMistakes: Using INNER JOIN on ProductSubcategory, which silently drops any order line for a product missing a subcategory
Joining to the wrong table's column (e.g. trying to reach ProductID directly from SalesOrderHeader, which doesn't have it)
Forgetting table aliases on a four-table query, making it unreadable and error-prone to debug
Not noticing that CustomerID on SalesOrderHeader maps to BusinessEntityID on Person.Person, not a column literally named CustomerID there
keyPoints: Each JOIN can reference any table already available earlier in the query, not just the first one
LEFT JOIN preserves rows that would otherwise be dropped by a stricter INNER JOIN
Mixing INNER and LEFT JOIN in one query is normal when different relationships have different guarantees
Clear aliases are essential once a query joins more than two or three tables

Uses LEFT JOIN specifically for ProductSubcategory

Explains why LEFT JOIN was chosen there instead of INNER JOIN

questions.title: Writing a groupBy/agg Aggregation in PySpark
questions.prompt: Write a PySpark transformation against a DataFrame named orders (columns: region, order_id, amount) that returns, for each region, the total amount and the count of orders, sorted by total amount descending.
questions.modelAnswer: groupBy("region") groups the rows by region, and .agg() lets you compute multiple aggregates in a single pass over the grouped data -- sum("amount").alias("total_amount") and count("order_id").alias("order_count"). Since groupBy/agg returns a new, unsorted DataFrame, .orderBy(col("total_amount").desc()) is needed afterward to get the descending order the question asks for. All of this builds a single lazy transformation plan; nothing actually executes until an action like .show() or .write() triggers it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this as one chain: group by region first, then agg() with both aggregates computed together rather than two separate groupBy calls, since agg() is built to take multiple aggregate expressions at once. I always import sum and count from pyspark.sql.functions with an alias (like _sum) so I don't accidentally shadow Python's own built-in sum and count, which is a subtle bug that's bitten people before. After the aggregation I chain orderBy with .desc() on the new total_amount column, because groupBy/agg's output isn't sorted by default -- people sometimes assume it comes back sorted by the aggregate just because that's what they asked for conceptually, but it's not, you have to ask for it explicitly.
questions.example:
from pyspark.sql.functions import sum as _sum, count, col

result = (orders
    .groupBy("region")
    .agg(
        _sum("amount").alias("total_amount"),
        count("order_id").alias("order_count")
    )
    .orderBy(col("total_amount").desc()))
commonMistakes: Shadowing Python's built-in sum/count by importing them without aliasing the pyspark.sql.functions versions
Using count("amount") when amount could be null, undercounting rows with a null amount instead of using count("*") or count(lit(1))
Forgetting agg() can compute multiple aggregates in one call instead of chaining multiple separate groupBy calls
Calling .show() before .orderBy(), assuming groupBy's output is already sorted by default
keyPoints: groupBy(column) groups rows; agg() computes one or more aggregates per group in a single pass
Aliasing aggregate functions from pyspark.sql.functions avoids shadowing Python built-ins
orderBy sorts the resulting aggregated DataFrame, which isn't sorted by default
The whole chain is a lazy transformation until an action triggers execution

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses groupBy with the right column
Correctly computes both aggregates in agg()
Correctly sorts descending by total amount
Avoids the built-in-shadowing/null-counting pitfalls

questions.title: Writing a MERGE INTO to Upsert Changed Customer Records
questions.prompt: You receive a daily batch of changed customer records in a DataFrame called updates (columns: customer_id, name, email, last_modified). Write the MERGE INTO statement (or DeltaTable Python API equivalent) that upserts these into an existing Delta table customers, matching on customer_id, updating name/email/last_modified when a match exists, and inserting the full row when it doesn't.
questions.modelAnswer: Using the DeltaTable Python API: get a handle on the existing table with DeltaTable.forName (or .forPath), then chain .merge(updates, "<matching condition>") with .whenMatchedUpdate(set={...}) and .whenNotMatchedInsert(values={...}), finishing with .execute(). The equivalent raw SQL MERGE INTO form is also a correct answer. The key detail either way: the matching condition must reference columns from both sides explicitly (using aliases), and whenMatchedUpdate's set dictionary maps target column names to source expressions, not the other way around.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for the DeltaTable API here since it reads cleanly in Python. First I get a handle on the target table, then alias both the target and the incoming updates DataFrame so the merge condition is unambiguous -- t.customer_id = s.customer_id. whenMatchedUpdate takes a dict mapping each target column to the source expression that should replace it, and whenNotMatchedInsert takes a similar dict for the full row to insert when there's no match. I always alias explicitly on both sides even though it's sometimes technically optional, because an unaliased merge condition on a four-plus-column table gets genuinely hard to read correctly at a glance.
questions.example:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "customers")

(target.alias("t")
    .merge(updates.alias("s"), "t.customer_id = s.customer_id")
    .whenMatchedUpdate(set={
        "name": "s.name",
        "email": "s.email",
        "last_modified": "s.last_modified"
    })
    .whenNotMatchedInsert(values={
        "customer_id": "s.customer_id",
        "name": "s.name",
        "email": "s.email",
        "last_modified": "s.last_modified"
    })
    .execute())
commonMistakes: Forgetting to alias both sides, producing an ambiguous column reference in the merge condition
Using whenMatchedUpdateAll()/insertAll() carelessly when the source has extra columns not present in the target, causing a schema mismatch
Writing the merge condition on a non-unique key, causing an error when multiple source rows match one target row
Running this as a plain overwrite/append instead of merge, losing existing unrelated customer rows or duplicating matched ones
keyPoints: DeltaTable.merge() (or SQL MERGE INTO) requires an explicit matching condition between aliased source and target
whenMatchedUpdate/whenNotMatchedInsert define exactly what happens on each outcome
The merge key must uniquely identify a row in the target for predictable behavior
This replaces a slower, non-atomic read-modify-write pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly constructs the merge condition on customer_id
Correctly writes whenMatchedUpdate with the right columns
Correctly writes whenNotMatchedInsert with the full row
Code is syntactically valid

questions.title: Cleaning Nulls Before an Aggregation
questions.prompt: A DataFrame shipments has a nullable delay_minutes column. Write PySpark code that replaces null delay_minutes with 0 before computing an average delay per carrier, and separately, write code that instead drops any row where carrier is null (a different, stricter requirement) before that same aggregation.
questions.modelAnswer: fillna (or .na.fill) replaces nulls in a specified column with a default value -- here, 0 for delay_minutes. dropna (or .na.drop(subset=[...])) instead removes entire rows where the specified columns are null, rather than substituting a value. These are not interchangeable for this scenario: filling delay_minutes with 0 changes the meaning of the resulting average -- a null delay becomes a zero-minute delay, not 'we don't know' -- while dropping rows on carrier removes those rows from the aggregate's denominator entirely. Conflating fillna and dropna is a real correctness bug, not just a style choice, because they produce different numbers.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write these as two clearly separate pieces of code, because they solve genuinely different problems even though both get called 'cleaning nulls.' For the first requirement, I'd use na.fill({'delay_minutes': 0}) scoped to that one column specifically, rather than a blanket fill, since I don't want to accidentally substitute 0 into some other nullable column that has nothing to do with this request. For the second, na.drop(subset=['carrier']) removes only rows where carrier itself is null, leaving everything else alone. The distinction I'd flag out loud: filling delay_minutes with 0 means a missing reading now counts as 'zero minutes late' in the average, which is a real assumption I'm making about what a null means there -- if that's not actually true, the average I just computed is subtly wrong, not just technically different from the drop-rows version.
questions.example:
from pyspark.sql.functions import avg

# Requirement 1: substitute 0 for null delay_minutes
clean = shipments.na.fill({"delay_minutes": 0})
result = clean.groupBy("carrier").agg(avg("delay_minutes").alias("avg_delay"))

# Requirement 2 (different): drop rows where carrier is null
filtered = shipments.na.drop(subset=["carrier"])
result2 = filtered.groupBy("carrier").agg(avg("delay_minutes").alias("avg_delay"))

questions.title: Deduplicating to the Latest Record Per Key
questions.prompt: A bronze table customer_updates has multiple rows per customer_id, each with a different updated_at timestamp, because every change was appended rather than updated in place. Write PySpark code that keeps only the single most recent row per customer_id.
questions.modelAnswer: The standard pattern is a Window partitioned by customer_id, ordered by updated_at descending, with row_number() assigning 1 to the most recent row per partition, then filtering to row number == 1. dropDuplicates(["customer_id"]) is explicitly the wrong tool here because it keeps an arbitrary row per key, not necessarily the most recent one -- it has no concept of 'most recent,' only 'first encountered.'
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic dedup-to-latest pattern, and I'd reach for a Window every time rather than dropDuplicates, specifically because dropDuplicates has no idea which row is newest -- it just keeps whichever one it happens to encounter first, which isn't a guarantee of recency at all. I'd partition the window by customer_id, order by updated_at descending so the newest row in each partition gets rank 1, add that as a helper column with row_number(), filter down to rn == 1, and then drop the helper column before handing the result off. The one thing I always double check is the sort direction -- ordering ascending instead of descending by mistake silently keeps the oldest row instead of the newest, and nothing about the output looks obviously wrong unless you know to check for it.
questions.example:
from pyspark.sql import Window
from pyspark.sql.functions import row_number, col

w = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(col("updated_at").desc())

latest = (customer_updates
    .withColumn("rn", row_number().over(w))
    .filter(col("rn") == 1)
    .drop("rn"))
commonMistakes: Using dropDuplicates(["customer_id"]) and assuming it keeps the most recent row (it keeps an arbitrary one)
Forgetting to order the window descending by updated_at, keeping the oldest row instead of the newest
Not dropping the helper rn column, leaving it in the final output
Using rank() instead of row_number(), which can return more than one row per customer if two updates share an identical timestamp
keyPoints: A Window partitioned by the key and ordered by the timestamp is the right dedup tool when 'most recent' matters
dropDuplicates has no sense of recency -- it keeps an arbitrary row per key
row_number() guarantees exactly one row per partition after filtering to rn == 1
The helper ranking column should be dropped from the final result

questions.title: Writing a Bicep Template for an Event Hub Namespace
questions.prompt: Write a Bicep resource declaration that provisions an Azure Event Hub Namespace on the Standard SKU, taking the namespace name and location as parameters. Explain what the resource's API version string is for, and why Bicep requires it explicitly.
questions.modelAnswer: A Bicep resource declaration takes the form resource <symbolicName> 'Microsoft.EventHub/namespaces@<api-version>' = {...}, with a sku block specifying name: 'Standard'. The API version string pins exactly which version of Azure's resource provider schema the declaration conforms to -- Azure resource types evolve their available properties across different API versions, and without specifying one explicitly there'd be no way to know which set of properties and behavior is actually being requested. Bicep (like the ARM templates it compiles to) requires it so deployments stay deterministic and reproducible rather than silently picking up whatever 'latest' happens to mean at deploy time, which could change behavior with no change to the template itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the resource block with namespaceName and location as parameters, defaulting location to resourceGroup().location since that's a common convenience. The part of the question worth actually explaining is the API version in the resource type string -- Microsoft.EventHub/namespaces@2022-10-01-preview, for example. That version isn't decoration, it's pinning exactly which schema of that resource type I'm asking for, because Azure resource providers add, remove, and change properties across versions. If Bicep let me skip it and just use 'whatever's current,' the same template could behave differently on two different days depending on what Azure shipped in between -- which is exactly the kind of non-determinism infrastructure-as-code is supposed to eliminate. So I treat picking an explicit, tested API version as part of the actual design decision, not a formality, and I don't bump it casually without checking for breaking changes first.

Hardcoding location instead of defaulting it to resourceGroup().location or taking it as a parameter
Confusing sku.name and sku.tier, or omitting one when the resource type requires both
Assuming a newer API version is always safe to bump to without checking for breaking property changes

questions.title: Writing a Redshift COPY Command From S3
questions.prompt: Write the Redshift COPY command that loads newline-delimited JSON files from an S3 prefix into a table named stg_orders, authenticating via an IAM role rather than embedded access keys, and explain why specifying an IAM role is the recommended authentication method.
questions.modelAnswer: The COPY command's basic shape is COPY <table> FROM '<s3-prefix>' IAM_ROLE '<role-arn>' FORMAT AS JSON 'auto' -- IAM_ROLE tells Redshift which role to assume when it reaches into S3 to read the files, rather than embedding a static access key and secret directly in the command text. Using an IAM role is recommended over access keys because the role's permissions are scoped specifically (read access to just the relevant bucket/prefix), its temporary credentials are automatically rotated by AWS rather than being long-lived secrets that could leak, and every COPY using that role is auditable through CloudTrail -- none of which is true for a hardcoded access key sitting in a script or saved query.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this the same way every time: COPY the target table, FROM the S3 path, IAM_ROLE naming the role's ARN, and FORMAT AS JSON 'auto' since these are newline-delimited JSON files. The IAM_ROLE piece is the part I'd actually explain if asked, because it's a real security decision, not boilerplate -- a role gives Redshift temporary, automatically-rotated credentials scoped to exactly what that role's policy allows, versus an access key, which is a long-lived secret that has to be manually rotated and, if it ends up in a script or in version control by accident, is a real credential sitting in plaintext somewhere. The role approach is also the one AWS actively recommends and what CloudTrail can cleanly audit back to a specific role's actions, which matters when something needs to be traced after the fact.

Granting the IAM role broader S3 access than the specific bucket/prefix actually being loaded from
Forgetting FORMAT AS JSON (or the matching format option) and leaving Redshift to misparse the files
Not handling malformed rows, letting one bad record fail the entire COPY instead of using a tolerance option deliberately

IAM_ROLE is the recommended authentication method over embedded access keys

questions.title: Writing a Step Functions State Machine That Runs a Glue Job Then Catches Failures
questions.prompt: Write the Amazon States Language (ASL) JSON for a Step Functions state machine with two main states: RunGlueJob (a Glue StartJobRun.sync task) followed by NotifySuccess, with a Catch block on RunGlueJob that routes any error to a NotifyFailure state instead of letting the whole execution fail silently.
questions.modelAnswer: The .sync suffix on the Glue StartJobRun resource ARN is what makes Step Functions actually wait for the Glue job to finish running before advancing to the next state -- without .sync, the task would be considered complete the instant the job was merely started, regardless of whether it later succeeded or failed. The Catch array on RunGlueJob specifies ErrorEquals (commonly ["States.ALL"] to catch any error type) and a Next pointing at a dedicated failure-handling state, so a job failure routes the execution somewhere deliberate -- a notification, a cleanup step -- rather than the whole state machine execution simply ending in a Failed status with nothing else happening. NotifySuccess and NotifyFailure are terminal states (each needs End: true, or its own Next if there's more after it) representing the two possible outcomes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always reach for the .sync pattern on a Glue job inside a state machine, because the non-.sync version is a trap -- it fires the job and immediately reports back as if its job is done, which means the state machine would move on to NotifySuccess before the Glue job has actually run at all. The Catch block is the other piece I treat as non-negotiable on anything that can genuinely fail -- without it, a job failure just terminates the whole execution with a Failed status and nothing else happens, no notification, no cleanup, nothing actionable. I'd catch broadly with States.ALL here since the question just wants any failure routed somewhere, though on a real production state machine I'd often want more specific error handling for different failure types. Each of the two outcome states needs an explicit End: true since they're not routing anywhere further.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the .sync suffix, so the state machine advances before the Glue job actually finishes
Omitting a Catch block entirely, letting any failure end the execution with no custom handling
Catching an overly narrow ErrorEquals list and missing failure types outside it
Forgetting End: true (or a Next) on a terminal state, which is required for a valid state machine definition
keyPoints: The .sync suffix makes Step Functions wait for the Glue job's actual completion
A Catch block routes a failure to a deliberate next state instead of ending the execution silently
ErrorEquals: ["States.ALL"] catches any error type for broad handling
Terminal states each require End: true or a further Next
