questions.title: Diagnosing a deadlock between two ETL jobs
questions.prompt: Two nightly stored procedures occasionally fail with a deadlock error when they run at overlapping times, each updating the same two tables. Explain what a deadlock is, how SQL Server resolves it automatically, and two concrete things you'd change to prevent it from recurring.
questions.modelAnswer: Blocking happens whenever one transaction needs a lock another transaction already holds, and simply waits -- this is normal and expected. A deadlock is the special case where Transaction A is waiting on a lock held by Transaction B, while B is simultaneously waiting on a lock held by A -- neither can ever proceed. SQL Server detects this automatically and picks one transaction as the 'deadlock victim,' rolling it back and raising an error, while the other transaction proceeds normally. To prevent recurrence: (1) access the two tables in the same order in both procedures -- a common deadlock cause is two transactions locking the same two tables in opposite order; and (2) keep transactions as short as possible, doing only what genuinely needs to be atomic inside BEGIN/COMMIT, so locks are held for the shortest possible window and the overlap that triggers the deadlock has a smaller chance of occurring.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by reassuring whoever's asking that blocking itself isn't a bug -- it's how isolation is enforced any time two transactions genuinely need the same data at the same moment. A deadlock is the specific, more serious case: A is waiting on a lock B holds, B is waiting on a lock A holds, and neither can ever win -- it's a true standoff. SQL Server doesn't just hang forever; it detects the cycle and picks a 'deadlock victim' to roll back automatically, which is why the application sees an error and needs to retry. For the actual fix, the first thing I'd check is whether both procedures touch the two tables in a different order -- that's the single most common cause, and standardizing the access order so both procedures always touch, say, Table A before Table B usually eliminates it outright. Second, I'd look at whether either transaction is doing more than it needs to inside BEGIN/COMMIT -- unrelated reads, validation logic -- and trim the transaction down to just the atomic part, since shorter transactions hold locks for less time and collide less often.
commonMistakes: Treating a deadlock the same as ordinary blocking -- blocking is normal, a deadlock is a genuine, unresolvable standoff
Assuming SQL Server will just hang forever instead of recognizing it auto-detects and resolves deadlocks
Fixing the symptom by adding a retry loop in the application without addressing the inconsistent table access order
Making a transaction longer by adding error handling or logging inside it, which increases lock duration
keyPoints: Blocking is normal; a deadlock is two transactions waiting on each other with no way out
SQL Server auto-detects deadlocks and rolls back a chosen 'victim' transaction
The victim's application should retry the transaction
Accessing tables in a consistent order across procedures prevents most deadlocks
Shortening transactions reduces how long locks are held and how often collisions occur

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes blocking from a deadlock

Proposes consistent table access order as a concrete fix
Proposes shortening transactions as a concrete fix

questions.title: A query got slow after it used to be fast
questions.prompt: A report query that filters WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013 used to run instantly and now takes minutes as the table has grown. There is an index on OrderDate. Diagnose why the index isn't helping, and rewrite the WHERE clause so it is.
questions.modelAnswer: The predicate is non-SARGable: wrapping the OrderDate column in the YEAR() function forces SQL Server to compute YEAR(OrderDate) for every single row before it can compare against 2013, which means the index on the raw OrderDate column can't be used -- it stores actual dates, not year-extracted values. This was barely noticeable on a small table (a full scan of a few hundred rows is instant either way), but as the table grows into the millions of rows, the same non-SARGable predicate turns a sub-second query into one that takes minutes. The fix is to rewrite the condition so the column itself is left untouched, and transform the comparison value instead: WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2014-01-01'. This asks the identical logical question but lets SQL Server use the index on OrderDate to jump directly to the matching range.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a textbook SARGability problem, and the giveaway is right there in the WHERE clause -- there's a function wrapped around the column. Any time I see YEAR(SomeDateColumn), UPPER(SomeColumn), or similar, my first instinct is: the index on that raw column can't be used, because SQL Server would have to transform every row's value before it could compare it, and an index doesn't store transformed values. The reason it 'used to be fast' is simply table size -- a full scan is invisible on a small table and brutal on a large one, so this kind of bug often doesn't show up until data volume grows past some threshold. The fix is always the same shape: stop transforming the column, and transform the comparison value instead. Instead of asking 'what year is this date in,' I ask 'is this date within the 2013 calendar year range' -- same answer, but now the raw OrderDate column is untouched in the comparison, so the existing index can be used for a range scan instead of a full scan.
commonMistakes: Blaming the index itself ('the index must be corrupt/fragmented') instead of the predicate wrapping the column
Rewriting to BETWEEN '2013-01-01' AND '2013-12-31' and accidentally excluding rows with a time component on Dec 31
Not recognizing other common non-SARGable patterns like UPPER(column) = 'X' or a leading-wildcard LIKE '%text'
Assuming the problem only appears with YEAR() and missing that any function on the column causes the same issue
keyPoints: SARGable means the predicate can use an index directly; non-SARGable forces a full scan
Wrapping the column in a function (YEAR, UPPER, etc.) makes a predicate non-SARGable
Fix by transforming the comparison value instead of the column
The performance gap only becomes visible as table size grows

questions.title: A report is hanging, but there's no deadlock error
questions.prompt: Users report that a dashboard query has been 'just spinning' for several minutes, but no deadlock error ever appears. Explain the difference between this situation and a deadlock, how you'd identify the actual head blocker, and what you'd check before deciding to kill the blocking session.
questions.modelAnswer: This is ordinary blocking, not a deadlock -- a deadlock is a genuine standoff that SQL Server detects and resolves automatically within seconds by killing a victim; it never just hangs indefinitely. Plain blocking, by contrast, can hang as long as whatever is holding the lock keeps holding it, because there's no cycle for SQL Server to detect -- one session is simply waiting its turn behind another, and nothing resolves that automatically. To find the actual head blocker, I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests, specifically looking at the blocking_session_id column -- the session with a non-zero blocking_session_id is being blocked, and the session that ID points to (which itself usually shows blocking_session_id = 0) is the head blocker actually holding the lock everyone's waiting on. Before killing that session, I'd check what it's actually doing -- its SQL text, and whether it's an open, uncommitted transaction (an application that opened a transaction and is sitting idle, or a long-running batch job that's legitimately mid-write). Killing a session mid-write rolls back whatever it was doing, which can be worse than the wait itself if it's a large, mostly-finished operation -- so I'd rather understand what it's doing and consider letting it finish or committing/rolling it back cleanly than reflexively kill it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd clarify, because it changes the whole response, is that this isn't a deadlock -- SQL Server resolves deadlocks on its own, usually within seconds, by picking a victim and rolling it back. If nothing has errored and the query is just sitting there, that's plain blocking: one session waiting on a lock another session is holding, with no cycle, so nothing forces a resolution automatically. My first query is always against sys.dm_exec_requests, looking at blocking_session_id -- that tells me directly who's blocked and, by following the chain, who the actual head blocker is, as opposed to the session that looks blocked but is itself only blocked by someone else further up. Once I've got the head blocker's session ID, I'd pull its actual SQL text and check whether it's sitting inside an open transaction that was never committed, versus genuinely mid-execution on a big write. That distinction decides what I do next -- if it's an application bug that opened a transaction and forgot to close it, killing the session is reasonable and I'd also flag that bug separately. If it's a legitimate long-running batch load that's 90% done, killing it rolls back all of that work and probably makes things worse, so I'd rather let it finish, or coordinate with whoever owns that job before touching it.
questions.example:
-- Find who's blocking whom
SELECT session_id, blocking_session_id, wait_type, wait_time, status
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests
WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0;

-- Follow the chain to the head blocker (blocking_session_id = 0, but others point to it)
-- Then inspect what the head blocker is actually running:
SELECT text
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests r
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) t
WHERE r.session_id = @HeadBlockerSessionId;
commonMistakes: Treating any hanging query as a deadlock, when a true deadlock is auto-resolved within seconds, not left hanging
Killing the first blocked session found instead of tracing blocking_session_id to the actual head blocker
Killing a session without checking whether it's mid-write on a legitimate long-running job
Not distinguishing an application bug (an abandoned open transaction) from a genuinely busy, legitimate session
keyPoints: A hanging query with no error is ordinary blocking, not a deadlock -- deadlocks auto-resolve quickly
sys.dm_exec_requests' blocking_session_id column traces the blocking chain to the actual head blocker
Check what the head blocker is actually doing before killing it -- an abandoned transaction vs. a legitimate long write
Killing a session mid-write rolls back its work, which can be worse than waiting for it to finish

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes ordinary blocking from a deadlock
Correctly identifies how to find the head blocker (sys.dm_exec_requests / blocking_session_id)
Explains what to check before killing the blocking session
Provides correct, relevant diagnostic SQL

questions.title: A Covering Index Isn't Helping, and Nobody Knows Why
questions.prompt: A table has a nonclustered index covering exactly the columns a report query needs, but the query's execution plan still shows a full scan instead of using the index. The query is SELECT * FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail WHERE ProductID = 712. What's the most likely cause, and how would you fix the query?
questions.modelAnswer: SELECT * is almost certainly the cause. A covering index only helps when the query asks for columns the index actually includes; SELECT * asks for every column in the table, regardless of what's actually needed, which defeats the index's coverage the moment even one requested column isn't part of it. SQL Server then has to fall back to either a Key Lookup for each matching row or a full scan, depending on cost, instead of satisfying the query entirely from the narrower index. The fix is to name only the columns the report genuinely needs instead of SELECT *: SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty, UnitPrice FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail WHERE ProductID = 712. If those four columns are exactly what the covering index includes, the optimizer can now satisfy the entire query from the index alone, without ever touching the underlying table.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before touching the index, I'd actually look at the execution plan and the exact columns requested, because 'should use the index but doesn't' almost always traces back to the SELECT list, not the index definition. SELECT * is the first thing I'd check, because it's such a common habit and such a direct cause: if the index only covers four specific columns and the query asks for all fifteen columns on the table via *, the index simply can't satisfy that request on its own, and SQL Server has to go fetch the rest from the table itself — either via a Key Lookup per row or by abandoning the index entirely for a full scan, depending on how many rows are involved. The fix is almost always just naming the specific columns the report actually displays instead of *. I'd also double check that the index's included columns genuinely match what the report needs, because if even one required column is missing from the index, the same fallback happens no matter how narrowly I write the SELECT list.
commonMistakes: Assuming the index itself must be broken or missing, without checking what columns the query actually requests
Rebuilding or recreating the index before checking the SELECT list, missing the actual cause
Not verifying the index's included columns genuinely cover everything the trimmed SELECT list needs
Fixing this one query but not checking other queries against the same table for the identical SELECT * habit
keyPoints: SELECT * requests every column, defeating a covering index that only includes some of them
The fallback is a Key Lookup per row, or a full scan, instead of satisfying the query from the index alone
The fix is naming exactly the columns actually needed
The index's included columns must still genuinely match what's requested for this fix to work

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies SELECT * as the likely cause
Correctly explains why it defeats a covering index
Provides a correct fix naming specific columns
Notes the fix depends on the index already covering those exact columns

questions.title: A Nightly Write Fails With a Schema Mismatch Error
questions.prompt: A nightly job that appends new rows to a Delta table silver_orders starts failing overnight with a schema mismatch error, after the upstream source added a new discount_code column. Explain why Delta Lake rejects this write by default, and the two different ways you could legitimately fix it depending on whether you actually want that new column kept.
questions.modelAnswer: Delta Lake enforces schema on write by default -- schema enforcement -- meaning any append whose DataFrame schema doesn't exactly match the target table's existing schema is rejected outright rather than silently reshaping either the data or the table; this is deliberate, protecting a table from silently absorbing bad or unexpected structure. Here the upstream source added a genuinely new column, discount_code, that the existing table has never seen, so the incoming DataFrame's schema no longer matches. Fix 1 (new column should be kept going forward): enable schema evolution for this specific write using the mergeSchema option (or ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMNS for an explicit, deliberate change), which adds discount_code to the table's schema and backfills it as null for all existing historical rows -- appropriate when the new column is a genuine, wanted addition to the table going forward. Fix 2 (new column should NOT be kept, at least not yet): explicitly drop the discount_code column from the incoming DataFrame before the write, keeping the existing schema exactly as it was -- appropriate if the column is premature, not yet reviewed, or not meant for this table at all. The wrong move in either case is turning off schema enforcement broadly or blindly enabling schema evolution everywhere, since that would also let a genuine upstream mistake (a renamed or malformed column) slip through unnoticed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain that this failure is actually Delta doing its job, not malfunctioning -- schema enforcement exists specifically to reject a write that doesn't match the table it's writing to, rather than silently reshaping either side. Here the real cause is upstream: a new discount_code column showed up that the table's current schema has never seen. From there it's genuinely a judgment call, not a single fix. If this column is something the team actually wants captured going forward, I'd enable schema evolution for this one write -- the mergeSchema option, or an explicit ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMNS -- which adds the column and backfills every existing row with null for it. If it's not something we want yet, maybe it's premature or hasn't been reviewed, I'd just drop it from the incoming DataFrame before writing, leaving the table's schema untouched. What I wouldn't do is turn on mergeSchema globally as a blanket setting, because that quietly removes the protection schema enforcement was giving us in the first place -- I want this to be a deliberate decision each time, not a default.
questions.example:
-- Fix 1: deliberately evolve the schema to add the new column
df.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("mergeSchema", "true").saveAsTable("silver_orders")

-- Fix 2: deliberately exclude the new column instead, keeping the existing schema
df.drop("discount_code").write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("silver_orders")
commonMistakes: Globally disabling schema enforcement instead of handling this one deliberate change
Using mergeSchema=true reflexively without first checking whether the new column is actually wanted
Confusing mergeSchema (adds new columns) with overwriteSchema (replaces the entire schema, used with overwrite mode)
Not considering that mergeSchema backfills existing rows with null for the new column, which may or may not be the right default
keyPoints: Schema enforcement rejects a write whose schema doesn't exactly match the target table by default, deliberately
mergeSchema=true (or ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMNS) is the fix when the new column should genuinely be added
Explicitly dropping the new column before the write is the fix when it shouldn't be kept yet
The decision should be deliberate per-write, not a blanket toggle

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why schema enforcement rejects the write
Correctly describes the mergeSchema/add-column fix and when it's appropriate
Correctly describes the drop-the-column fix and when it's appropriate
Warns against a blanket/reflexive fix

questions.title: Yesterday's Numbers Changed After the Fact
questions.prompt: A gold-layer daily sales summary for Tuesday showed $42,000, but when the same report is rerun on Thursday, Tuesday's number has quietly changed to $45,800, with no code deployment in between. Walk through the most likely explanation and what you'd check to confirm it.
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely explanation is late-arriving data: some source records for Tuesday's sales didn't actually land in the bronze layer until after Tuesday's pipeline run had already processed and aggregated the day, and when the pipeline re-ran on a later day and reprocessed or re-aggregated Tuesday's partition, those late rows were now present and included, changing the total. This is common with upstream systems that batch-export with their own delay, or with retries/corrections applied after the fact. To confirm: check the bronze layer for Tuesday's partition at two points in time -- the row count/content as of when Tuesday's original gold number was computed versus the row count now -- if the bronze count for Tuesday's partition genuinely grew between those two checks, that confirms late-arriving data rather than, say, a bug in the aggregation logic itself (which would typically affect many days' numbers, not just reshape one specific day inexplicably). Also check whether the pipeline's silver/gold logic actually reprocesses historical partitions on each run (which exposes it to late data) versus only ever appending the current day (which wouldn't have changed Tuesday at all) -- understanding which processing model is in place is itself diagnostic information about whether this is even possible.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first instinct is late-arriving data, not a code bug, specifically because nothing was deployed between the two runs -- if the logic itself hadn't changed, the most plausible explanation for a number changing is that the underlying data changed. I'd go check Tuesday's partition in the bronze layer and compare its row count now against what it would have had to be at the time the original $42,000 number was computed, which I can often reconstruct from pipeline run logs or a bronze-layer audit column. If that count genuinely grew, that confirms it -- some rows for Tuesday simply hadn't arrived yet when the first pass ran. I'd also check whether this pipeline's design even reprocesses historical partitions on each run or only ever appends the newest day, because that tells me whether late data reaching Tuesday's partition after the fact was even possible given how the pipeline is built, versus pointing me toward a different explanation entirely if it's append-only.
commonMistakes: Assuming a code bug changed the number without first checking whether the underlying source data itself changed
Not distinguishing a pipeline that reprocesses historical partitions from one that only appends new data, which changes what's even possible here
Treating a 'the number changed and we don't know why' report as acceptable instead of tracing the root cause before reporting a new number as correct
Not considering that late data could keep arriving, meaning even the new Thursday number for Tuesday might not be final
keyPoints: Late-arriving source data reprocessed into a historical partition is the most common explanation for a day's number changing after the fact
Confirm by comparing bronze-layer row counts/content for that date across two points in time
Whether the pipeline reprocesses historical partitions versus only appends matters to the diagnosis
A number that already changed once may not be fully final, which is worth flagging

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies late-arriving data as the likely cause
Describes a concrete way to confirm it (comparing bronze layer over time)
Distinguishes a reprocessing pipeline design from an append-only one
Notes that the number may still not be final

questions.title: terraform apply Is Stuck Saying the State Is Locked
questions.prompt: A teammate's terraform apply crashed partway through (their laptop lost power) and now every terraform plan or apply anyone on the team runs fails immediately with a state lock error. Explain what the lock is actually protecting against, why it's now stuck, and the right way to resolve it versus the risky shortcut people sometimes take.
questions.modelAnswer: Terraform's state lock exists to prevent two people (or two CI runs) from modifying the same state file concurrently, which could otherwise corrupt the state or produce a result where Terraform's recorded idea of infrastructure no longer matches reality -- it's a safety mechanism, not a bug getting in the way. Normally the lock is acquired at the start of a plan/apply and released automatically when it finishes; the problem here is that the laptop lost power mid-apply, so the process that held the lock never got to release it cleanly, leaving the lock held indefinitely with no actual operation still running. The right way to resolve it is terraform force-unlock <lock-id>, using the specific lock ID shown in the error message -- but critically, only after confirming no apply is actually still running somewhere (checking with the teammate, checking CI, checking the backend directly if it's something like an Azure Storage blob lease) -- force-unlocking while an apply genuinely is still in progress elsewhere is the risky shortcut, because it can let two applies run concurrently against the same state after all, defeating the entire purpose of the lock and risking real corruption. Separately, it's worth checking whether the crashed apply left any resources partially created that the state doesn't yet reflect, since a mid-apply crash can also cause state drift independent of the lock issue.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the lock isn't an obstacle, it's doing exactly what it's supposed to do -- preventing two plan/apply operations from touching the same state file at the same moment, which could otherwise corrupt it or leave it out of sync with real infrastructure. The reason it's stuck is simple: the process that held the lock never got to release it, because the laptop lost power before the apply finished. The right fix is terraform force-unlock with the specific lock ID from the error message, but I'd never run that without first confirming nothing else is genuinely still applying -- checking with the teammate directly, checking whether any CI job is mid-run, maybe checking the backend's lock state directly if that's possible. Force-unlocking while something actually is still running defeats the whole point of having a lock and risks two applies racing against the same state, which is a much worse problem than being temporarily blocked. I'd also take a look at whether the crashed apply left anything half-created in real infrastructure that the state file doesn't know about yet, since that's a separate drift issue the lock alone won't reveal.
commonMistakes: Running terraform force-unlock reflexively without first confirming no apply is genuinely still running elsewhere
Deleting the state file's lock entry manually in the backend instead of using force-unlock with the correct lock ID
Not checking for resources partially created by the crashed apply that might now be drifted from state
Treating the lock as a bug to work around rather than a safety mechanism doing its job
keyPoints: The state lock prevents concurrent modifications that could corrupt state or desync it from real infrastructure
A crashed process can leave the lock held indefinitely with nothing actually running
terraform force-unlock with the specific lock ID is the correct fix, but only after confirming nothing is genuinely still running
A crashed mid-apply can also leave real state drift worth checking for separately from the lock itself

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the purpose of the state lock
Correctly explains why it's stuck after the crash
Correctly describes force-unlock as the fix, with the safety check first
Mentions checking for state drift from the crashed apply

questions.title: A Glue Crawler Keeps Creating Separate Tables Instead of One
questions.prompt: A Glue Crawler pointed at an S3 prefix with daily-partitioned Parquet files (s3://bucket/orders/year=2026/month=01/day=15/...) is creating a new table in the Data Catalog every few days instead of one orders table with partitions. Diagnose the likely cause and the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: The crawler decides whether a set of files belongs to one logical table (as partitions) or to separate tables based on how similar their inferred schemas and folder structure are; this usually breaks down because of schema drift across days -- a new column appeared, an existing column's type changed, or the folder depth/naming became inconsistent -- which makes the crawler conclude the files are different enough to be separate tables rather than partitions of one. The fix starts upstream: enforce one consistent schema and partition-key naming convention across every day's export, so the crawler's similarity check actually succeeds. It also helps to explicitly configure the crawler's schema-change behavior (update the existing table's schema, or add new columns, rather than leaving it to create a new table object whenever it detects drift), and in some cases to define the table explicitly up front instead of relying purely on crawler inference for an actively evolving source.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is to actually compare the folder structure and a sample of the schema across a few of the days that ended up as separate tables versus days that grouped together correctly, because the crawler's grouping logic is really just a similarity check -- if that check fails, it defaults to 'these are different tables.' The usual culprit is schema drift: someone added a column partway through, or a type changed from string to int for the same column on a different day, or the partition folder naming went from year=2026/month=01/day=15 to something slightly different. Once I've confirmed which it is, the actual fix is upstream -- getting the source export to produce a consistent schema and consistent partition structure every day -- plus checking the crawler's own configuration for how it's set to handle schema changes, since by default it may be creating a new table rather than updating the existing one's schema when it sees drift.
commonMistakes: Assuming the crawler is simply broken instead of checking for schema or folder-structure drift across days
Not comparing the actual schema/folder structure between days that grouped correctly and days that didn't
Fixing only the Catalog by merging/deleting tables without addressing the upstream drift that keeps causing it
Leaving the crawler's schema-change behavior on its default instead of configuring how it should handle detected drift
keyPoints: The crawler groups files into one table (as partitions) based on schema and structure similarity
Schema drift or inconsistent partition folder naming across days is the most likely cause
The real fix is enforcing consistency upstream, not just cleaning up the Catalog after the fact
The crawler's schema-change handling setting controls whether drift updates or fragments the table

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies schema/structure drift as the likely cause
Describes a concrete way to confirm it (comparing days)
Proposes a fix addressing the upstream inconsistency
Mentions the crawler's schema-change configuration option

questions.title: An Athena Query Stopped Pruning Partitions and Costs Are Climbing
questions.prompt: A nightly Athena query against a table partitioned by order_date (a string column, 'YYYY-MM-DD') used to scan a few GB per run. After someone changed the WHERE clause to WHERE CAST(order_date AS DATE) = CURRENT_DATE - 1, it now scans the entire multi-terabyte table every night. Diagnose why, and rewrite the WHERE clause so partition pruning works again.
questions.modelAnswer: Athena's partition pruning works by matching the WHERE clause's predicate directly against partition metadata before it ever reads a single data file, and it can only do that when the partition column appears unmodified in the comparison. Wrapping order_date in CAST(... AS DATE) means Athena can no longer directly compare the raw partition values (which are stored as strings) against the condition -- it would have to evaluate that cast per-partition first, and in practice this defeats pruning entirely, falling back to scanning every partition, which is effectively the whole table. The fix is to stop transforming the partition column and instead express the comparison value in the same string format the partition is actually stored in: WHERE order_date = CAST(CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1' DAY AS VARCHAR) or, more simply, precompute the literal date string and compare order_date directly against it.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the same underlying mistake as wrapping a column in a function in a traditional SQL WHERE clause, just showing up as partition pruning instead of an index seek -- the mechanism is different, but the lesson is identical: don't transform the column, transform the comparison value. Here, order_date is stored as a string partition value, and CAST(order_date AS DATE) forces Athena to evaluate that cast before it can compare, which means it can't use partition metadata to skip folders upfront and ends up scanning everything. The fix is just removing the cast from the column side and expressing CURRENT_DATE - 1 as a string in the same 'YYYY-MM-DD' format the partitions are actually named in, so the comparison lines up directly against partition metadata with no evaluation needed first.
commonMistakes: Wrapping the partition column itself in a function, defeating Athena's ability to prune by metadata alone
Assuming Athena behaves like a database with indexes rather than scanning files directly based on partition metadata
Not checking that the rewritten literal's format exactly matches how the partition values are actually stored
Noticing the cost/time increase without tracing it back to the specific WHERE clause change that caused it
keyPoints: Partition pruning requires the partition column to appear unmodified in the WHERE clause
Wrapping the column in a function (like CAST) forces a fallback to scanning every partition
The fix is transforming the comparison value, not the column, matching the partition's stored format
This is the same SARGability-style principle as traditional SQL indexing, applied to partition metadata

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the CAST on the partition column as the cause
Correctly explains why this defeats partition pruning
Provides a correct, equivalent rewrite that restores pruning
Rewrite's literal format matches the partition's actual string format

questions.title: A Lambda-Based File Processor Starts Timing Out on Larger Files
questions.prompt: A Lambda function triggered by S3 ObjectCreated events has worked fine for months, parsing and loading each uploaded CSV into Redshift. Lately it's been hitting timeout errors, and the failures line up with days when upstream started sending noticeably larger files. Diagnose the root cause and propose two realistic fixes -- one quick, one more durable.
questions.modelAnswer: Lambda has a hard maximum execution duration (15 minutes) and a fixed memory/CPU ceiling per invocation. A function that parses and loads an entire file synchronously inside one invocation scales its runtime roughly with file size, so as upstream files cross some threshold, the identical code that worked fine on small files now exceeds the time or memory ceiling and gets killed mid-execution -- the code didn't break, the input simply grew past what Lambda's execution model was ever meant to handle in one shot. Quick fix: raise the function's memory allocation (which also increases its proportional CPU share) and its timeout toward the 15-minute ceiling -- this buys real headroom immediately, but it's a ceiling, not a scaling fix, and the same failure returns once files grow further. Durable fix: move the actual parsing/loading work to a Glue ETL job, a Spark-based engine with no fixed per-invocation time or memory ceiling that scales with data volume, and reduce Lambda's role to simply triggering that Glue job (directly, or via Step Functions) rather than doing the heavy processing itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment I hear 'this used to work and now it times out, and it correlates with bigger files,' I'm thinking about Lambda's hard ceilings -- 15 minutes max runtime, and a memory limit that also caps available CPU. A function processing a file end-to-end in one invocation is implicitly betting that files will stay small enough to finish within those ceilings, and that bet just stopped paying off. The fast fix, if I need something today, is bumping memory and timeout -- memory bump helps CPU too, which often matters more than people expect for CPU-bound parsing work. But I'd be upfront that this is buying time, not solving the actual problem; it'll hit the wall again once files grow past the new ceiling. The fix I'd actually want to land is moving the heavy lifting off Lambda entirely and onto Glue, which is built for exactly this kind of job and doesn't have Lambda's fixed per-invocation ceiling -- Lambda's job becomes just reacting to the S3 event and kicking off the Glue job, which is squarely what Lambda is good at.
commonMistakes: Treating repeated timeouts as a flaky, one-off issue instead of a scaling ceiling being hit
Raising the timeout to the 15-minute maximum without also checking memory, missing half the fix
Assuming a quick timeout/memory bump is a permanent solution rather than a stopgap
Concluding Lambda is wrong for any S3-triggered workflow, when the real fix is Lambda-triggers-Glue, not removing Lambda entirely
keyPoints: Lambda has fixed execution-duration (15 min) and memory/CPU ceilings per invocation
A file-size-dependent workload can outgrow those ceilings even if the code never changed
Raising memory/timeout is a legitimate quick fix but not a durable scaling solution
Moving the heavy processing to Glue, with Lambda only triggering it, is the durable fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies Lambda's time/memory ceilings as the root cause
Proposes a realistic quick fix (memory/timeout increase)
Proposes a realistic durable fix (offloading to Glue)
Notes the quick fix's limitation as a stopgap, not a permanent solution

questions.title: A DMS CDC Task Is Falling Further Behind Every Hour
questions.prompt: A DMS task replicating ongoing changes (CDC) from an on-premises SQL Server to a Redshift target has a steadily growing CDC latency metric in CloudWatch -- it was near zero at migration cutover and is now hours behind. Walk through what you'd check, in order, to find the bottleneck.
questions.modelAnswer: First, check CloudWatch's CDCLatencySource versus CDCLatencyTarget metrics specifically, since they isolate which half of the pipeline is actually behind: CDCLatencySource rising means DMS is struggling to keep up reading changes from the source's transaction log; CDCLatencyTarget rising means DMS is reading changes fine but failing to apply them to the target fast enough. If source-side: check whether the source database's transaction log retention/growth is an issue, and whether the DMS replication instance itself (CPU, network throughput, allocated storage) is undersized for the current change volume -- a replication instance sized for the original one-time bulk load is not necessarily sized correctly for sustained ongoing CDC volume. If target-side: check whether Redshift writes are competing with other concurrent load/COPY activity through workload management queues, whether the target table is missing sort/distribution keys that would make applies faster, or whether DMS is applying changes in small, inefficient batches rather than larger ones. Across either path, also check whether the change volume itself has simply grown since cutover -- the original sizing decision may no longer match current reality regardless of any new problem.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start with the one metric that tells me which half of the pipeline to even look at: CDCLatencySource versus CDCLatencyTarget in CloudWatch. If source latency is the one climbing, the replication instance isn't keeping up reading from the source's transaction log -- I'd check the instance's own CPU/network/storage sizing, since what was right-sized for the initial bulk migration load isn't automatically right-sized for ongoing day-to-day change volume. If it's target latency that's climbing, DMS is reading changes fine but Redshift is the slow part -- I'd check whether applies are competing with other load jobs for WLM queue slots, whether the target table's distribution/sort keys are actually helping writes land efficiently, and whether DMS is batching applies reasonably or trickling them in one at a time. Either way, I'd also just sanity-check whether the source's actual transaction volume has grown since cutover -- sometimes there's no new problem at all, the original instance sizing simply hasn't kept pace with a business that's now doing more volume than it was when the sizing decision was made.
commonMistakes: Not checking CDCLatencySource vs. CDCLatencyTarget first, guessing at the bottleneck instead of isolating which side it's on
Assuming the replication instance sized for the initial bulk load is automatically correct for sustained CDC
Overlooking target-side contention (concurrent Redshift load jobs competing for WLM queue slots)
Treating a growing change-volume trend as a bug rather than an outgrown sizing decision
keyPoints: CDCLatencySource vs. CDCLatencyTarget isolates which half of the pipeline is behind
Source-side issues usually trace to replication instance sizing or transaction log pressure
Target-side issues usually trace to Redshift write contention, missing keys, or small apply batches
Change volume growing since cutover can itself outgrow an originally correct sizing decision

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly starts with CDCLatencySource/Target to isolate the bottleneck side
Proposes relevant source-side checks
Proposes relevant target-side checks
Considers growth in change volume as a factor

questions.title: Choosing a clustering key for a new fact-staging table
questions.prompt: You're designing a new staging table that will be loaded nightly and queried immediately afterward by ProductID ranges. A table can have only one clustered index. Explain the difference between a clustered and nonclustered index, and what makes a good choice of clustering key.
questions.modelAnswer: A clustered index determines the actual physical order rows are stored in on disk -- which is exactly why a table can have only one: data can only be physically sorted one way. A nonclustered index is a separate structure that holds a sorted copy of the indexed column(s) plus a pointer back to the actual row, and a table can have many of them. Looking up a row through the clustering key is fastest, since SQL Server navigates directly to the physical location; looking up through a nonclustered index takes one extra step -- find the index entry, then follow the pointer back to the row. A good clustering key is narrow (a small data type, since every nonclustered index secretly stores the clustering key as its row pointer), unique (no ambiguity about physical order), and ever-increasing (so new rows append at the end instead of forcing existing rows to physically shuffle). Given the staging table is loaded nightly and then range-queried by ProductID, an ever-increasing identity key for the clustered index, with a nonclustered index on ProductID to support the range queries, is the more defensible design than clustering directly on ProductID.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this as two separate decisions. First: what should the table's physical row order be -- that's the clustered index, and I only get one shot at it. Second: what other lookup patterns do I need to support cheaply -- that's where nonclustered indexes come in, and I can have several. For a staging table that's loaded nightly, I actually lean toward an ever-increasing identity column as the clustering key rather than ProductID directly, even though ProductID is the column people will query by. The reason is load performance: an ever-increasing key means new rows always append at the end of the physical order, so the nightly load doesn't cause page splits from inserting into the middle of existing data. Then I add a nonclustered index on ProductID to support the range queries -- yes, that costs one extra pointer-following step per lookup compared to clustering directly on ProductID, but it's a much smaller cost than the load-time page-splitting I'd get from clustering on a column that isn't naturally ordered or unique.
commonMistakes: Assuming more indexes are always better without considering the nightly load's insert cost
Choosing a wide, non-unique column as the clustering key, which bloats every nonclustered index that secretly carries it as a pointer
Forgetting a table can have only one clustered index, and trying to 'cluster' on two different columns
Not connecting the ever-increasing key recommendation to the specific nightly-load write pattern described in the scenario
keyPoints: Clustered index = physical row order, one per table
Nonclustered index = separate structure with a pointer back to the row, many allowed
Good clustering key: narrow, unique, ever-increasing
Design choice should weigh load (insert) pattern against query (read) pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the clustered vs. nonclustered distinction
Correctly lists the three traits of a good clustering key
Applies the tradeoff to the specific nightly-load scenario given
Recommends a nonclustered index to support the ProductID range queries

questions.title: Designing the Medallion Layers for a New IoT Sensor Feed
questions.prompt: A manufacturing client wants to onboard a new IoT sensor feed (temperature readings every 10 seconds from 500 machines) into their existing medallion lakehouse. Propose what bronze, silver, and gold should each look like for this specific feed, and call out one design decision that's genuinely different from a typical daily batch source.
questions.modelAnswer: Bronze should capture the raw sensor events essentially as received -- machine_id, timestamp, temperature_reading, and whatever metadata the feed includes, partitioned by ingestion date, appended via a streaming write (Autoloader or Structured Streaming) rather than a batch job, since the feed is continuous, not a daily drop. Silver should deduplicate (sensor feeds commonly resend due to retries), validate/flag out-of-range readings rather than silently dropping them (a sensor reporting -200°C is itself a signal, likely a hardware fault worth tracking, not just bad data to discard), and conform timestamps to a consistent timezone/format. Gold should aggregate to a business-relevant grain -- likely per-machine, per-hour (or per-shift) average/min/max temperature -- rather than exposing raw 10-second readings to dashboards, since nobody queries individual readings directly and the aggregation also dramatically reduces the row count a BI tool has to handle. The genuinely different design decision from a typical daily batch source: this pipeline should be built with Structured Streaming (bronze-to-silver, possibly silver-to-gold) rather than a scheduled batch job, because the whole value of 500 machines reporting every 10 seconds is lost if the pipeline only processes once a day -- but that also means handling late-arriving/out-of-order events and watermarking decisions that a daily batch job never has to think about at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design bronze to take the feed almost exactly as it arrives -- machine ID, timestamp, reading, whatever metadata comes with it -- ingested continuously via Autoloader or Structured Streaming rather than a nightly job, because batching a 10-second feed once a day throws away the entire reason it reports that often. Silver is where I'd dedupe, since sensor retries sending the same reading twice is common, and I'd flag rather than discard anything wildly out of range, because a reading of -200°C is probably a broken sensor, which is itself useful information, not noise to filter out. Gold I'd aggregate to something a dashboard can actually use -- per-machine hourly min/max/average, not 500 machines' worth of raw 10-second points. The thing I'd flag as genuinely different here versus a normal batch source is that this whole pipeline needs to think about late and out-of-order events and watermarking, which a once-a-day batch job simply never has to deal with -- that's a real design cost that comes with the territory of actually getting streaming's value.
commonMistakes: Treating this like any other batch source and scheduling it nightly, losing the real-time value of a 10-second feed
Silently dropping out-of-range sensor readings in silver instead of flagging them as a potential hardware-fault signal
Exposing raw 10-second-grain readings directly to gold/dashboards instead of aggregating to a usable grain
Not considering deduplication in silver, when sensor/IoT feeds commonly resend due to network retries
keyPoints: Bronze should ingest the raw feed via streaming, not batch, given the continuous nature of the source
Silver should deduplicate and flag (not silently discard) out-of-range readings
Gold should aggregate to a usable grain (per-machine, per-hour) rather than exposing raw readings
Streaming ingestion introduces late/out-of-order event handling that a daily batch source wouldn't need

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a sensible bronze design appropriate to a streaming source
Proposes a sensible silver design including dedup and handling out-of-range values
Proposes a sensible gold aggregation grain
Correctly identifies the streaming-vs-batch design difference and its implications

questions.title: Moving a Team Off Local Terraform State
questions.prompt: A data platform team of six engineers has been running terraform apply from individual laptops with local state files, and it's already caused two incidents where someone applied against a stale state. Propose the fix, and explain specifically what remote state with locking adds that local state doesn't have.
questions.modelAnswer: The fix is moving to a remote backend (for an Azure-based platform, typically an Azure Storage Account container configured as the backend) with state locking enabled, rather than each engineer holding their own local terraform.tfstate file. Local state has two compounding problems: first, there's no single source of truth -- six engineers' local state files can each represent a different, possibly stale, idea of what infrastructure actually exists, so an apply from one laptop can act on an outdated picture and either fail to detect real drift or, worse, try to recreate/modify something another teammate already changed; second, there's no locking at all -- nothing prevents two people from running apply concurrently against their own (different) local copies, each racing to mutate real infrastructure with no coordination whatsoever. A remote backend fixes the first problem by giving everyone the same, current state file, read from and written to one shared location on every plan/apply. The locking a remote backend adds on top fixes the second: it acquires an exclusive lock for the duration of a plan/apply, so a second engineer's concurrent attempt is blocked (or informed) until the first one finishes, rather than both operations racing against the same shared state simultaneously -- which is actually a sharper danger with shared remote state than with disconnected local files, so locking isn't optional once state is centralized.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd move the team to a remote backend with locking, and I'd explain the fix as solving two separate problems the incidents already revealed. Local state means there's no single source of truth -- six people, six potentially different ideas of what actually exists, and an apply from any one laptop can act on a stale picture without anyone knowing until something breaks. A remote backend fixes that by centralizing to one shared, always-current state file everyone's plan and apply reads from and writes to. But centralizing alone isn't enough -- once everyone's pointed at the same shared state, now I need locking, or two people running apply at the same moment race against that one file instead of just having their own separate stale copies, which is actually a worse failure mode than what they have now. The lock that comes with most remote backends acquires exclusively for the duration of an apply, so a second attempt waits its turn instead of colliding. I'd also plan the migration carefully -- each engineer's existing local state needs to be migrated into the new backend cleanly, not just abandoned, so nothing gets lost in the transition.
commonMistakes: Moving to remote state without also enabling locking, which trades 'divergent local state' for 'concurrent corruption of one shared state'
Not migrating each engineer's existing local state into the new backend cleanly (terraform init -migrate-state), risking state loss
Assuming remote state alone prevents bad applies, when it only provides a shared source of truth and locking, not approval/review
Forgetting to restrict direct backend access so engineers can't still bypass the shared state by reverting to local
keyPoints: Local state means no single source of truth across a team, risking stale-state applies
Local state also has no locking, allowing concurrent applies to race against different copies
Remote state centralizes to one shared, current state file everyone reads/writes
Locking (part of most remote backends) prevents concurrent applies from racing against the shared state

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes remote backend with locking as the fix
Correctly explains the stale/divergent local state problem
Correctly explains what locking specifically adds (preventing concurrent corruption)
Notes the migration/rollout consideration

questions.title: Designing the Zones of an S3-Based Data Lake for a Glue/Athena Pipeline
questions.prompt: You're designing the S3 layout for a new batch pipeline that lands raw vendor CSV exports, cleans them with Glue, and serves curated results to Athena and Redshift Spectrum. Propose a zone structure and explain what belongs in each zone, and why keeping the original raw files matters even after they're transformed.
questions.modelAnswer: A raw zone holds the vendor files exactly as received -- immutable, partitioned by ingestion date, never edited in place -- serving as the pipeline's one faithful source of truth that allows reprocessing if a downstream transformation later turns out to be wrong. A processed (or cleaned) zone holds data after Glue has applied type casting, deduplication, and consistent partitioning, typically converted to Parquet, still close to record-level grain. A curated (or analytics-ready) zone holds data shaped for specific consumption -- aggregated or denormalized tables that Athena and Redshift Spectrum query directly, usually registered as their own tables in the Glue Data Catalog. Keeping the raw files matters because a transformation bug discovered weeks later can only be fixed correctly by reprocessing from a faithful original; if raw files were overwritten or deleted once processed, that ability is permanently lost -- the same reasoning the bronze/silver/gold medallion pattern is built on, just with AWS-native zone names.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd lay this out as three zones with very different jobs. Raw is the zone I never touch after it lands -- vendor files exactly as they arrived, partitioned by ingestion date, nothing cleaned or cast yet. Processed is where Glue actually does the cleaning -- consistent types, dedup, converted to Parquet -- but I'd keep it close to the original record grain rather than jumping straight to a report's shape, since other things might need this same clean data later. Curated is the layer actually built for Athena and Redshift Spectrum to query directly -- aggregated or denormalized specifically for how it'll be consumed. The reason I insist on keeping raw around even after everything's processed: the day someone finds a bug in the processed-zone transformation logic, I want to be able to reprocess from an untouched original, not from data that already baked in the mistake. Skipping that and processing in place destroys the one thing that would let me cleanly fix a mistake discovered after the fact.
commonMistakes: Overwriting or discarding raw files once they've been processed, losing reprocessing ability
Skipping the processed zone and aggregating straight from raw into curated, losing a reusable record-level layer
Applying business-specific aggregation logic in the processed zone, coupling a shared layer to one consumer's needs
Not registering curated tables in the Glue Data Catalog, making them awkward for Athena/Spectrum to discover
keyPoints: Raw preserves vendor data exactly as received, enabling reprocessing
Processed applies cleaning/standardization while staying close to record grain
Curated is shaped specifically for how Athena/Redshift Spectrum will consume it
Keeping raw intact protects against unrecoverable mistakes discovered downstream

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a sensible raw zone design and purpose

questions.title: Lambda, Glue, or EMR: Choosing the Right Compute for Three Different Jobs
questions.prompt: You have three workloads to design compute for: (1) resizing a thumbnail every time an image lands in S3, (2) a nightly ETL job transforming 200GB of order data with several joins and aggregations, (3) a one-time migration requiring custom Hadoop-ecosystem tools (Hive, HBase) that Glue doesn't expose. Which AWS compute service fits each, and what's the deciding factor each time?
questions.modelAnswer: (1) Lambda: a small, fast, event-triggered task comfortably within Lambda's time and memory ceilings, where paying per invocation beats running any kind of cluster for work this size. (2) Glue: a managed, serverless Spark environment purpose-built for ETL, with Data Catalog integration and job bookmarks that make incremental loads straightforward -- the right size for a substantial but standard nightly batch ETL job. (3) EMR: the deciding factor is needing the broader Hadoop ecosystem -- Hive, HBase, Presto, custom cluster bootstrap actions -- that Glue's managed Spark environment doesn't expose; EMR trades more operational responsibility for full control over the cluster and its ecosystem. The deciding factor each time is really: task size/duration against Lambda's hard ceiling, whether it's a standard Spark ETL pattern that fits Glue's managed sweet spot, or a genuine need for ecosystem flexibility that only EMR's cluster control provides.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame each choice around what's actually driving it, not a general preference. The thumbnail resize is squarely Lambda -- small, fast, event-triggered, and spinning up any kind of cluster for a job that finishes in seconds would be wasteful both in cost and complexity. The nightly 200GB ETL job is Glue's sweet spot -- it's exactly the standard Spark ETL pattern Glue is built for, and I get the Data Catalog integration and job bookmarks for incremental loads without managing any cluster infrastructure myself. The one-time migration needing Hive and HBase specifically is where I'd reach for EMR, because that's the actual deciding factor -- Glue's managed Spark environment simply doesn't expose that ecosystem, and EMR gives me a real cluster I can configure with whatever tools the migration needs, at the cost of more operational work than Glue would ever require.
commonMistakes: Using Lambda for a job that's genuinely too large or long-running for its 15-minute, fixed-memory ceiling
Reaching for EMR by default for standard ETL, taking on unnecessary cluster-management overhead Glue would have handled
Assuming Glue exposes the full Hadoop ecosystem (Hive, HBase, etc.) the way a raw EMR cluster does
Choosing compute based on familiarity rather than the workload's actual size, pattern, and ecosystem needs
keyPoints: Lambda fits small, fast, event-triggered tasks within its time/memory ceiling
Glue fits standard, substantial Spark ETL without needing to manage cluster infrastructure
EMR fits workloads needing the broader Hadoop ecosystem or full cluster control Glue doesn't expose
The deciding factor is task size/duration, ETL pattern fit, or ecosystem/control needs -- not habit

Correctly matches Glue to the nightly ETL workload with reasoning
Correctly matches EMR to the ecosystem-dependent migration with reasoning

questions.title: Designing a Near-Real-Time Clickstream Pipeline With Kinesis
questions.prompt: A product team wants near-real-time (under 5 minutes) visibility into website clickstream events, eventually landing in S3 for Athena queries while also feeding a live dashboard. Propose an architecture using Kinesis, and explain the specific role Kinesis Data Streams and Kinesis Data Firehose each play, rather than using just one of them.
questions.modelAnswer: Kinesis Data Streams is the ingestion layer the application writes events to directly, and its real value here is giving multiple independent consumers their own read position over the same stream -- a live-dashboard consumer and a separate delivery-to-S3 consumer can each read the same events independently, which Firehose alone has no concept of, since it isn't built for multiple independent replaying consumers. Kinesis Data Firehose is then configured as one specific consumer of that stream, buffering and batching records before reliably delivering them to S3 at the size/time intervals configured, and handling format conversion (e.g., to Parquet) that would otherwise have to be custom-built. The proposed flow: events written to Kinesis Data Streams (shared ingestion) -> consumed independently by both the live-dashboard path and a Firehose delivery stream -> Firehose delivers batched, converted data to S3 -> Athena queries it there. Using Data Streams alone would mean building custom delivery/batching/retry logic for the S3 path; using Firehose alone would mean no second consumer could independently tap the same real-time events for the live dashboard.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd put Kinesis Data Streams at the front because the real requirement here is that the same events need to reach two different places independently -- a live dashboard and an S3 landing zone for Athena -- and Data Streams is specifically built to let multiple consumers each read the stream on their own schedule without stepping on each other. Firehose is not a substitute for that; it's the piece I'd hang off Data Streams as one specific consumer, handling exactly the 'reliably batch and deliver to S3, converting to Parquet along the way' job, which would otherwise be a decent amount of custom code to build and maintain myself. So the shape is: events into Data Streams, dashboard reads directly from the stream for its near-real-time view, and a Firehose delivery stream also reads from it to land batched, Parquet-converted data in S3 for Athena. I wouldn't collapse this to just Firehose, because then the dashboard has no independent way to tap the same events.
commonMistakes: Using Firehose alone and assuming it supports multiple independent consumers the way Data Streams does
Using Data Streams alone and custom-building the S3 delivery/batching/format-conversion logic Firehose already provides
Not considering that the dashboard and the S3 delivery path need genuinely independent read access to the same events
Underestimating the under-5-minute requirement and defaulting to a batch (non-streaming) design
keyPoints: Kinesis Data Streams enables multiple independent consumers to read the same event stream
Kinesis Data Firehose handles reliable batching, delivery, and format conversion to a destination like S3
The two serve different roles and typically combine rather than substitute for each other
This combination directly satisfies the near-real-time, dual-consumer requirement in the scenario

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains Data Streams' multi-consumer role
Correctly explains Firehose's batching/delivery role
Proposes a coherent end-to-end architecture satisfying both consumers
Explains why using only one of the two services falls short

questions.title: Redshift Provisioned Cluster or Redshift Serverless?
questions.prompt: Two teams are each choosing between a provisioned Redshift cluster and Redshift Serverless: Team A runs predictable, steady analytical workloads nearly 24/7; Team B runs occasional ad hoc analysis a few hours a week with long idle stretches in between. Which would you recommend to each, and what's the actual cost/operational tradeoff driving the choice?
questions.modelAnswer: For Team A, a provisioned cluster, sized and ideally reserved appropriately, is typically more cost-effective, because Serverless's per-second billing for compute capacity used is priced for variable or intermittent usage, and a workload running nearly around the clock is better served by a fixed, often reservation-discounted cluster than paying Serverless's premium per-unit rate continuously. For Team B, Redshift Serverless is the better fit, because it scales down to effectively no charge during the long idle stretches and scales up automatically the moment a query actually runs, versus a provisioned cluster that bills continuously whether anyone is querying it or not -- paying for a cluster sitting mostly idle through the week is wasted spend. The actual deciding factor is utilization pattern, not team size or workload complexity: continuous, predictable usage favors provisioned (cost-efficient at scale, operationally stable); spiky, infrequent usage favors serverless (no idle cost, automatic scaling, less capacity planning).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd recommend based entirely on utilization pattern, not anything else about the two teams. Team A is running something close to continuously, which is exactly the case where a provisioned cluster wins on cost -- a fixed, reservation-eligible cluster running 24/7 is cheaper than paying Serverless's per-second rate around the clock, and the operational stability of a known, sized cluster is also a real plus for a steady workload. Team B is the opposite case -- a few hours a week with long idle gaps -- and a provisioned cluster there means paying for capacity that's sitting unused nearly all the time. Serverless is built for exactly that: it costs essentially nothing while idle and scales up automatically the moment a query runs. I'd be explicit that this decision comes down to utilization shape, not workload complexity or team size -- a team with a genuinely complex but steady workload still wants provisioned, and a team with simple but bursty usage still wants serverless.
commonMistakes: Recommending Serverless for every team by default because it sounds more modern or hands-off
Recommending a provisioned cluster for a bursty, mostly-idle workload, paying for unused capacity
Basing the recommendation on workload complexity or team size rather than actual utilization pattern
Not considering reserved-instance discounts when comparing provisioned cost against Serverless for steady usage
keyPoints: Provisioned clusters suit continuous, predictable workloads more cost-effectively
Serverless suits spiky, infrequent workloads by scaling to near-zero cost when idle
The deciding factor is utilization pattern, not team size or workload complexity
A provisioned cluster running idle most of the time represents real wasted spend

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends provisioned for Team A with sound reasoning
Correctly recommends Serverless for Team B with sound reasoning
Correctly identifies utilization pattern as the actual deciding factor
Avoids basing the recommendation on irrelevant factors (team size, complexity)

questions.title: Replacing a Cron-and-Shell-Script Pipeline With Step Functions
questions.prompt: An existing pipeline runs as a chain of cron jobs on an EC2 instance: a shell script kicks off a Glue crawler, waits an arbitrary sleep period, then triggers a Glue ETL job, then (if that succeeded) triggers another job to refresh an Athena view. It's fragile and nobody's confident it handles failures correctly. Propose how you'd redesign this with Step Functions, and specifically what the sleep-based waiting is covering for that Step Functions does properly instead.
questions.modelAnswer: Redesign as a Step Functions state machine with each stage -- the crawler run, the first ETL job, the second ETL job -- as its own state, using the .sync service integration pattern for the Glue crawler-start and StartJobRun actions, so Step Functions actually waits for genuine completion before advancing, rather than the cron script's arbitrary sleep, which is really just a guess at 'how long this usually takes' -- it either wastes time waiting longer than necessary, or, worse, advances before the job has actually finished on a day it happens to run long. Step Functions also gives each state proper Catch/Retry handling, so a transient failure in the crawler or a job can retry automatically with backoff, and a genuine failure routes to an explicit failure/notification state instead of the shell script either silently continuing with stale data or failing with no clear record of why. The visual, per-execution history Step Functions keeps is also a real operational improvement over grepping through a cron job's log file to reconstruct what happened.
questions.professionalAnswer: The sleep is the giveaway that this pipeline was never actually synchronized -- it's standing in for 'wait until the previous step is truly done,' and a fixed sleep can only ever approximate that, never guarantee it. I'd redesign this as a state machine with the crawler run, first ETL job, and second ETL job each as their own state, using the .sync integration pattern so each state genuinely waits for its action to finish rather than assuming a guessed duration. That alone removes the fragility the sleep was covering for. On top of that, I'd add Catch and Retry to each state, so a transient blip in the crawler or a job gets retried automatically instead of silently derailing the whole chain, and a real failure routes to an explicit notification state instead of the shell script just failing with a log line nobody's watching. I'd also point out the operational upside of Step Functions' execution history -- when something does go wrong, there's a visual record of exactly which state failed and why, instead of reconstructing it from a cron log after the fact.
commonMistakes: Keeping an arbitrary sleep/wait inside a redesigned pipeline instead of using a .sync integration pattern
Not adding Catch/Retry handling, reproducing the original pipeline's fragility in a new tool
Assuming Step Functions alone fixes reliability without actually configuring proper failure routing
Overlooking the Glue crawler as its own state needing the same .sync treatment as the ETL jobs
keyPoints: An arbitrary sleep is a guess at duration, not a genuine completion signal
The .sync integration pattern makes Step Functions wait for genuine completion of each step
Catch/Retry handling replaces silent failure with automatic retries and explicit failure routing
Step Functions' execution history is a real operational improvement over parsing cron logs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes a state machine with .sync integration for each stage
Correctly explains what the sleep was standing in for and why that's fragile
Proposes Catch/Retry handling for failures
Notes the operational visibility improvement over cron/shell logs

questions.title: Designing Least-Privilege IAM Roles Across a Multi-Service Pipeline
questions.prompt: A pipeline chains S3 -> Glue -> Redshift -> Athena, each step reading the previous step's output. A new hire suggests giving the Glue job's IAM role full S3 access and full Redshift access "so we don't have to debug permissions issues." Explain why that's the wrong default, and what a least-privilege version of each role in this chain should actually look like.
questions.modelAnswer: A full-access role violates least privilege and turns any single compromised credential or buggy job into a blast radius covering the entire pipeline's data, not just what that component actually needs -- if the Glue job's role can write anywhere in Redshift, a bug in that job, or a compromised credential for it, can touch tables far outside its actual responsibility. A least-privilege version: the Glue job's role gets S3 read access scoped specifically to the source bucket/prefix it reads and S3 write access scoped to the specific output prefix it writes, plus a narrowly scoped Redshift/Secrets Manager permission limited to the specific cluster and database credential it actually loads into -- not account-wide access to either service. Each later step in the chain (the role behind the Redshift COPY, the role behind Athena/Glue Catalog reads) gets its own narrowly scoped role rather than everything reusing one broad role. The 'debugging is easier with full access' argument trades an ongoing real security risk for a one-time convenience; the actual fix for permission-debugging friction is testing with a scoped role from the start and reading the specific Access Denied error message, which names the exact missing permission -- not avoiding scoping altogether.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on that suggestion directly, because 'full access so we don't have to debug' is trading a real, ongoing security exposure for a one-time convenience that isn't even that large. If the Glue job's role can touch anything in S3 and anything in Redshift, then a bug in that job, or a leaked credential for it, can now reach data across the entire pipeline instead of just what it's actually supposed to touch. What I'd set up instead: the Glue job's role gets read access scoped to just its specific source prefix, write access scoped to just its specific output prefix, and a Redshift permission scoped to the one cluster and credential it actually loads into -- nothing account-wide. Every other step in the chain gets its own similarly scoped role rather than everyone sharing one broad one. On the actual debugging concern, scoped roles aren't actually harder to debug once you're used to it -- an Access Denied error names the exact permission that's missing, which is a faster diagnosis than trying to figure out, after an incident, what a full-access role actually touched.
commonMistakes: Granting broad or account-wide access 'to avoid debugging friction' instead of scoping and reading specific Access Denied errors
Reusing one shared role across every step in the pipeline instead of giving each step its own scoped role
Scoping S3 access by bucket only, when scoping to the specific prefix is both possible and tighter
Treating least privilege as a one-time setup task rather than something to revisit as the pipeline's steps change
keyPoints: A full-access role turns any single bug or leaked credential into a pipeline-wide blast radius
Each step's role should be scoped to only the specific resources/prefixes it actually needs
Different steps in a chain should get separate, independently scoped roles, not one shared role
Access Denied errors name the specific missing permission, making scoped-role debugging tractable

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why full access is the wrong default (blast radius)
Proposes concrete, scoped permissions for the Glue job's role
Proposes separate scoped roles for other steps rather than one shared role
Addresses the debugging-convenience argument directly
